28	## 1. Research objective
29	Estimate the causal effect of adopting an LLM agent assistant (Cursor) on project-level development velocity and software quality in open-source GitHub projects, and test how velocity and quality interact over time [A] (p. 1, p. 2).
30	
31	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
32	- Single RQ: "How does the adoption of LLM agent assistants impact project-level development velocity and code quality?" [V] (p. 2).
33	- No formal hypotheses are stated. The panel-GMM part tests four causal paths: lines added → warnings, lines added → complexity, complexity → next-month lines added, warnings → next-month lines added (Equation 7) [V] (p. 6).
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: observational, quasi-experimental difference-in-differences (DiD) with staggered adoption. *DiD* compares how an outcome changes over time in adopters versus non-adopters, so that trends affecting both groups cancel out. Cursor adopters are compared with never-adopters matched by propensity score (1:3 nearest neighbour, same primary language) [V] (p. 4, p. 5). Main estimator: Borusyak et al. imputation estimator, chosen because two-way fixed effects (TWFE) can be biased under staggered adoption with heterogeneous effects [V] (p. 6). Pre-trend (placebo) tests use heteroscedasticity- and cluster-robust Wald tests on h = −6..−2; h = −1 is dropped for anticipation [V] (p. 6). Velocity–quality interactions are tested with Arellano-Bond dynamic panel GMM (two-step, first-difference, repository + month fixed effects, lags 2–3 as instruments) [V] (p. 6, p. 8).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: "treatment" = first commit touching `.cursorrules` or `.cursor` files, used as a proxy for adopting the modern (Composer/agentic) Cursor client [V] (p. 2, p. 4). Treatment is intent-to-treat: actual usage intensity, LLM backend and Cursor version are unknown [V] (p. 7).
38	- Baselines or comparison conditions: matched never-adopter repositories plus not-yet-treated adopters. The comparison is against "state-of-the-practice" (controls may use Copilot or ChatGPT without visible traces), not against no AI use [V] (p. 7). Robustness: TWFE and Callaway & Sant'Anna estimators (Appendix B) and subsets by usage intensity, activity level, other AI tools, language and adoption cohort (Section 4.3, Appendix C) [V] (p. 9, p. 15, p. 16, p. 17).
39	
40	## 4. Dataset and sample
41	- Data source(s): GitHub code search API (Cursor config files), GHArchive monthly event data (matching covariates), GitHub API (primary language), local SonarQube Community server (outcomes and lines of code) [V] (p. 4, p. 5).
42	- Sample size (N) and unit: unit = repository-month. 23,308 Cursor files in 3,306 non-fork repos were found; the ≥10-star filter leaves 806 adopting repos [V] (p. 4). The text states 1,380 matched controls [V] (p. 2); Table 7 "Original" setting lists 801 treatment repos, 1,172 control repos, 21,699 observations and 4,481 post-treatment observations [V] (p. 17). GMM models use 14,755 observations [V] (p. 8). Primary languages: TypeScript 366, Python 118, JavaScript 60, Go 36, Rust 24 repos [V] (p. 4).
43	- Sampling / selection method: all discoverable repos with Cursor config files and ≥10 stars (threshold cited as 97% precision for engineered projects); adoption dates Jan 2024–Mar 2025; still available Aug 2025 [V] (p. 4). Matching pool: all GitHub repos with ≥10 stars, ~760k–820k candidates per monthly cohort, at most 10,000 sampled per cohort; logistic propensity models with 6 monthly lags plus cumulative history; AUC 0.83–0.91, McFadden pseudo-R² 0.14–0.27 [V] (p. 4, p. 14). Balance: all normalised differences |ND| < 0.25 ("acceptable"), but raw mean gaps remain large (e.g. pull requests 1,075.58 vs 266.03; age 496 vs 681 days, ND −0.207) [V] (p. 14). No power analysis reported.
44	- Data availability (public? link?): replication package at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18368661 [V] (p. 11).
45	
46	## 5. Experimental setup
47	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: monthly outcomes and covariates Jan 2024–Aug 2025, giving ≥6 months pre/post for treated repos; unbalanced panel [V] (p. 5). Time-varying covariates: lines of code, age, contributors, stars, issues opened (issue comments dropped for collinearity, ρ > 0.7) [V] (p. 5). All outcomes log-transformed; ATT read as 100(e^ATT − 1)% [V] (p. 7). SonarQube version and quality profile (rule set): not reported.
48	- Code availability: replication package on Zenodo (p. 11); its contents are not described in the paper.
49	
50	## 6. Evaluation metrics
51	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
52	  - Commits per month; lines added per month — development velocity; common productivity proxies with moderate-to-strong correlation with perceived productivity [V] (p. 5).
53	  - Static analysis warnings — total count of SonarQube reliability, maintainability and security issues; framed as an estimate of review effort because static analysis has false positives [V] (p. 5).
54	  - Duplicated line density — % duplicated lines (SonarQube; usually ≥10 consecutive statements or 100 tokens) [V] (p. 5).
55	  - Code complexity — total SonarQube cognitive complexity of the codebase; chosen as better aligned with understandability than cyclomatic complexity [V] (p. 5).
56	  - The three quality metrics were chosen from a technical-debt perspective because they can be computed at scale from version control [A] (p. 5).
57	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): ATT with standard errors and ± ranges on the % change; significance at 0.05/0.01/0.001; robust Wald pre-trend tests; GMM with Sargan (instrument validity) and AR(1)/AR(2) tests [V] (p. 7, p. 8). No correction for multiple comparisons across 5 outcomes × many subsets is reported.
58	
59	## 7. Key findings
60	1. Main DiD (Borusyak): lines added +28.58% (±13.7%, p < 0.05); commits +2.63% (n.s.); static analysis warnings +30.26% (±6.66%, p < 0.001); duplicated line density +7.03% (n.s.); code complexity +41.64% (±7.62%, p < 0.001) — [V] (p. 7). Significance stars were read from the PDF image; the text extraction attaches *** to every cell.
61	2. The velocity gain is transient: only months 1–2 are significant; commits +55.4% / +14.5% and lines added +281.3% / +48.4% in months 1 / 2 — [V] (p. 8, Figure 3).
62	3. Quality effects persist to month 6 for warnings and complexity; all outcomes pass the pre-trend tests — [V] (p. 8, Figure 3).
63	4. Panel GMM: velocity does not significantly raise warnings or complexity; Cursor has no significant direct effect on warnings (−0.011) once codebase size is controlled; Cursor still raises complexity (0.086, p < 0.01, reported as a "9% baseline increase") — [V] (p. 8, Table 3).
64	5. Panel GMM: a 100% increase in complexity or warnings goes with a 64.5% / 50.3% decrease in next-month lines added; Cursor gives a 1.84x baseline increase in lines added; ~3x complexity or ~5x warnings would cancel the gain — [V] (p. 8).
65	6. Robustness: quality effects are stronger in high-usage subsets (contributors who touched Cursor files made ≥80% of commits; months with config edits); they persist in very active repos and with/without traces of other AI tools (382 treated repos show other tools, 345 of them Copilot) — [V] (p. 9, p. 10, Figure 4).
66	7. Estimator sensitivity: TWFE agrees (warnings +18.48%, complexity +26.04%, both p < 0.001), but Callaway & Sant'Anna gives negative, non-significant quality estimates (warnings −10.49%, complexity −3.80%); the authors conclude the quality findings need caution — [V] (p. 16, Table 6).
67	8. Descriptive warning analysis (convenience sample, 195,010 warnings from 933 rules, 20-category taxonomy): 16/20 categories rise post-adoption; largest Naming Conventions +21.32, Code Hygiene +16.15, Code Complexity +15.34, Code Style +14.76 new warnings per repo per month; Logic Error +2.09, Security +1.98; API Usage −4.35 — [V] (p. 18, Table 8).
68	9. The authors interpret that much of the warning increase runs through velocity → codebase size → technical debt, so Cursor "may not necessarily introduce more code quality issues than non-adopting projects moving with the same velocity", whereas complexity is inherently higher in Cursor code — [A] (p. 10).
69	
70	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
71	- [A] Treatment covers only repos that commit Cursor config files; possible selection bias in either direction (p. 7).
72	- [A] Usage intensity and persistence unknown; estimates are intent-to-treat (p. 7).
73	- [A] Cursor version and LLM backend unknown (argued to raise external validity) (p. 7).
74	- [A] Matching is imperfect; unobserved confounders (expertise, team practices, culture) are untestable (p. 7, p. 14).
75	- [A] Contamination by other AI tools in both groups; the effect is relative to current practice, not to no AI (p. 7).
76	- [A] External validity: other agents, proprietary projects, languages beyond JS/TS/Python; fast-changing tools (p. 7); Java, C/C++, Rust insufficiently covered (p. 16).
77	- [A] Quality metrics may not capture the multi-dimensional nature of quality; complexity metrics were designed for human-written code (p. 11).
78	- [A] Estimators disagree for quality outcomes; many cohorts have fewer than 100 repos (p. 16).
79	- [A] Composer use and agentic use cannot be separated (p. 2, p. 17).
80	- [A] The warning-category analysis is a convenience sample and descriptive only (p. 18).
81	
82	## 9. Limitations we identified
83	- [I] Internal inconsistencies in reported numbers: the discussion cites a "25.1%" complexity increase attributed to Table 2 (p. 10) and a "25%" increase attributed to Table 3 (p. 11), while Table 2 reports +41.64% and Table 3 a 0.086 coefficient (~9%) (p. 7, p. 8). Probably left over from an earlier version; use the table values.
84	- [I] Sample counts differ between text and tables: 806 treated and 1,380 controls (p. 2, p. 4) versus 801 treated and 1,172 controls in Table 7 (p. 17). The paper does not explain the difference.
85	- [I] Warnings and complexity are repository totals, so they scale with codebase size; in the GMM, lines of code absorbs most variance and removes the direct Cursor effect on warnings (p. 8). "+30% warnings" is therefore mainly "more code", not a higher warning density. For RQ3 the per-code quality signal is complexity, not warnings. Based on Table 3 (p. 8).
86	- [I] The headline quality result depends on the estimator (Borusyak/TWFE positive; Callaway–Sant'Anna negative and n.s.) (p. 16); the abstract does not mention this.
87	- [I] Cursor-generated code is not identified at file or line level; quality changes are attributed to whole repositories, including human-written code.
88	- [I] The warning taxonomy was produced by the first author together with Claude Opus 4.5 (p. 18); no inter-rater or validation check is reported.
89	- [I] No functional-correctness or test outcome is measured; quality is static analysis only.
90	
91	## 10. Threats to validity
92	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): selection into treatment by committing config files; ITT dilution; unobserved confounders despite matching and fixed effects; anticipation handled by dropping h = −1 (p. 6, p. 7). Pre-trend tests pass for the main estimator (p. 8). Balance acceptable but imperfect (p. 14).
93	- External (generalisability of sample/context): open-source, ≥10-star GitHub repos, mostly TypeScript/Python/JavaScript; one tool (Cursor); mid-2024 to mid-2025 (p. 4, p. 7, p. 11). [I] No enterprise or reconstruction setting.
94	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): lines added and commits are rough velocity proxies; SonarQube warnings include false positives and are framed as review effort; cognitive complexity is a whole-codebase sum (p. 5, p. 11). [I] Maintainability is not measured directly (e.g. change effort by later developers).
95	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): no power analysis; many outcome × subset comparisons without correction; standard errors and ± ranges reported; estimator sensitivity for quality outcomes (p. 7, p. 16).
96	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): Zenodo replication package (p. 11); estimators and model specifications given as equations (p. 4, p. 6, p. 14, p. 15); SonarQube version/rule set not reported.
97	
98	## 11. Future research directions
99	- Stated by authors [A]: replicate with other and newer LLM coding tools (p. 7); test whether transient gains and proportional debt generalise to enterprise settings (p. 11); study why LLMs produce overly complex code and develop readability-aware fine-tuning or simplification passes (p. 11); study duplication under heavy AI use (p. 10); study other programming languages (p. 16); find the causes of warning-category increases (p. 18); design tools with quality assurance as a first-class feature, e.g. self-throttling (p. 11).
100	- Suggested by us [I]: measure quality per line or per file for AI-attributed changes instead of repository totals; pair static-analysis metrics with a downstream maintainability task (as borg2026echoes does) to test whether higher cognitive complexity actually slows later evolution.
101	
102	## 12. Relevance to our research
103	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (main), RQ4, RQ5.
104	- How it informs our work [I]: the strongest real-world causal evidence in our set that agentic, vibe-coding-style development raises code complexity and static-analysis warnings at project level. It does not study reconstruction from UI/behaviour, so it informs RQ3 by analogy only. Methodologically it shows the metric choices (SonarQube warnings, cognitive complexity, duplication) and why size normalisation and estimator robustness matter, which a reconstruction study should copy (RQ4/RQ5).

3	status: ready
4	evidence_basis: full-text
5	design: automated benchmark construction (LLM mine-craft-patch pipeline) + evaluation of 9 coding agents on partial and 3 agents on full web-app reconstruction from a live reference
6	dataset: ProgramDistill, 26 interactive web apps (18 OSWorld-derived, 8 open-source clones); 1,975 replay-verified browser behaviours; 4,063 repair tasks
7	sample_size: partial: 300 tasks x 9 models (1 run each); full: 12 apps x 3 models = 36 runs, 590 atomic + 413 cumulative behaviour tests
8	metrics: binary score and chain score from deterministic browser-trace replay; atomic behaviour recovery; cumulative workflow recovery; cost per trajectory; failure categories; shortcut-attempt rate
9	main_finding: Agents rebuild web apps from a live reference only partly: best full-app rebuild passes 49.2% of cumulative workflows; partial-repair success falls sharply as more dependent behaviours must be restored.
10	relevance: high
11	analysed: 2026-11-11

13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
17	
18	# ProgramDistill: From Interactive Web Apps to Verifiable Reference-Guided SWE Tasks
19	
20	- Authors: Kim, Jeonghye; Kim, Minseon; Kim, Young Jin; Pereira, Matheus; Côté, Marc-Alexandre; Sordoni, Alessandro; Yuan, Xingdi; Shi, Zhengyan
21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed; v1 dated 16 Sep 2026). Affiliations: KAIST, Microsoft Research Montréal, Microsoft AI (p. 1).
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.18805 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18805
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Evaluate coding agents on "reference-guided" software engineering: inferring intended behaviour by interacting with a working web application, then implementing it in an incomplete or empty application. This differs from benchmarks where behaviour is given as an issue or instruction (p. 1).
30	- [A] Turn working interactive web apps into a scalable, automatically built source of verifiable tasks ("application-to-task factorization") with controllable difficulty ("restoration depth") (p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [A] Guiding question: "Can we uncover this latent behavioral structure and use it to turn a working interactive web application into a scalable source of verifiable software-engineering tasks?" (p. 2). [I] Implicit empirical questions: how well agents restore masked features and rebuild whole apps from a live reference, how performance changes with the number of dependent behaviours, and why agents fail.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] A fully automated LLM pipeline ("mine–craft–patch") builds tasks; two evaluation settings follow, plus trajectory and failure analyses (p. 2; p. 6).
37	- Approach / model / intervention:
38	  - [V] *Mine*: LLM agents (Planner, Collector, Relabeler, Reflector), with read access to the source and the live app, propose behaviour goals, drive the app through a Playwright browser helper, and record replayable traces of actions plus expected observable signals (accessible names, visible text, URL, state). A trace is admitted only if it replays deterministically from a reset state (p. 3; p. 4; p. 25).
39	  - [V] *Craft*: an LLM masks (deletes) the source implementing a behaviour, either logic only or logic plus UI. A mask is accepted only if the app still builds, prerequisite traces still pass, the target trace fails, and an LLM "mask-depth critic" judges the deletion substantive. Masks along a prerequisite lineage are combined into cumulative tasks, and the reversed mask is the gold patch, which must replay the whole lineage (p. 4; p. 5; p. 6).
40	  - [V] *Patch*, partial-application reconstruction: the agent gets the masked repository, an LLM-written behavioural problem statement, and browser access to the live reference (no reference source, no internet) (p. 6).
41	  - [V] *Patch*, full-application reconstruction: the agent starts from a minimal scaffold plus a product-level capability description and must rebuild the whole app from the live reference (p. 6; p. 10; p. 11).
42	  - [V] All construction stages use GPT-5.6 Sol (p. 2; p. 7).
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 frontier models compared on partial reconstruction; 3 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) on full reconstruction. Logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks; restoration depths 1–8 (p. 8; p. 11). No human or non-agent baseline.
44	- [I] Relation to our topic: full-application reconstruction is very close to our scenario of rebuilding a web application by observing its UI and behaviour, with no access to its source. Partial reconstruction resembles restoring missing features in an existing codebase by consulting a working product.
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] 26 self-contained web apps: 18 adapted from the OSWorld web-application suite and 8 real-world open-source projects or SaaS clones (Actual Budget, Reactive Resume, Baserow, two Trello clones, two Jira clones, a Calendly clone), using Django, Angular, React and Next.js with SQL and document back ends. Each is pinned to a commit (p. 19).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit:
49	  - [V] Mining: 2,800 candidate goals, 2,350 collected, 2,165 reproduced and 1,975 verified behaviours; maximum lineage depth 17 (mean 3.40) (p. 7).
50	  - [V] Tasks: 4,063 in total, 2,862 atomic and 1,201 cumulative; 1,997 logic-only and 2,066 logic-and-UI (p. 7).
51	  - [V] Per-app task counts are very uneven, from 2 (ExpenseFlow) to 372 (Reactive Resume) (p. 19).
52	  - [V] Evaluation suite ProgramDistill-300: 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks covering 269 lineages and all 26 apps (p. 8).
53	  - [V] Full reconstruction: 12 apps, 590 atomic and 413 cumulative behaviour tests, 36 runs (p. 11; p. 12).
54	- Sampling / selection method: [V] ProgramDistill-300 is stratified by restoration depth (quotas 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 25 for depths 1–8) and selected round-robin across apps (p. 8). [I] Why these 26 apps, and why these 12 for full reconstruction ("twelve stateful web applications", p. 11), is not explained beyond "complementary sources" (p. 3).
55	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We are working on a public release of the ProgramDistill benchmark" (p. 1). Not yet released at time of writing; prompts are given in the appendix (p. 25; p. 30; p. 33).
56	
57	## 5. Experimental setup
58	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Modified R2E-Gym harness with tools `execute_bash`, `file_editor`, `search` and `finish`. A browser CLI drives both the reference and the current app (p. 8). Agents see only structured text observations (visible text, element IDs, roles, accessible names, input values); full reconstruction additionally exposes selectors. Screenshots and raw HTML are excluded (p. 3; p. 24).
59	- [V] Partial reconstruction: reasoning effort high, at most 1,000 steps, 150k-token history cutoff. Full reconstruction: reasoning effort max, at most 10,000 steps, 500k-token cutoff. Per-tool timeout 90 s, no aggregate time limit (p. 24).
60	- [V] Determinism: application state is reset before each collection and replay, and a shared fake clock (libfaketime plus a browser Date offset) is used (p. 3; p. 19; p. 20).
61	- [V] Isolation: the reference is reachable only via the browser helper, public egress is blocked, there is no pre-mask git history, and grading traces are private. Submissions are rebuilt and replayed in a fresh verifier (p. 10; p. 23; p. 24).
62	- [V] The full-reconstruction scaffold requires an `app.js` exporting `async function handle(req, res, context)`, with state kept in `context.state` (p. 37).
63	- [V] Number of runs: one per model and task (partial) and one per model and app (36 full-reconstruction runs, p. 12). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
64	- [V] Cost: tokens x LiteLLM list prices (p. 37). One GPT-6 Astra pass over 300 tasks took about 557 minutes on 4 servers (p. 37).
65	- Code availability: [A] release in progress (p. 1).
66	
67	## 6. Evaluation metrics
68	- Replay verifier V(A, L): returns 1 only if every recorded browser action completes and every expected signal is satisfied, replaying the whole prerequisite lineage without LLM involvement (p. 4).
69	- Binary score: 1 only if the complete lineage passes after the agent's patch. Chain score: fraction of repair targets passed, giving partial credit (p. 6).
70	- Full reconstruction: atomic behaviour recovery (fraction of single-behaviour tests passed, with prerequisites replayed) and cumulative workflow recovery (binary and chain) (p. 6; p. 11).
71	- [V] Source-level matching is not required: function names, variables and structure may differ if behaviour replays (p. 6). [V] In full reconstruction, however, selectors and accessible names must match the reference, because evaluation "replays user interactions using selectors" (p. 35).
72	- Diagnostics: interaction counts (observation, read/search, edit/write steps), share of unchanged target files and retained stub lines, shortcut-attempt rate, failure categories (p. 9; p. 10; p. 12).
73	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; means only. Pearson correlations between prompt size and binary score are reported in the context-length check (p. 40).
74	
75	## 7. Key findings
76	1. [V] Partial reconstruction (ProgramDistill-300): mean binary score is 84.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 68.7% for Claude Opus 5 and 60.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with a middle tier at 45.3–48.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview lowest at 22.3%. Mean cost per trajectory is $33.99, $28.86 and $16.01 for the top three (p. 8; p. 38).
77	2. [V] Success drops with restoration depth: Astra falls from 100% at depth 1 to 64.0% at depth 8, Opus 5 from 96% to 32.0% and Sol from 92% to 32.0%; every other model keeps less than half of its depth-1 performance (p. 8; p. 9).
78	3. [V] Restoring UI as well as logic is harder. Binary scores for logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks are 92.9% vs 76.9% for Astra and 76.4% vs 46.9% for Sol (p. 38).
79	4. [V] Full-application reconstruction (12 apps): Astra recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows, Opus 5 42.03% and 28.81%, and Sol 33.39% and 21.07% (p. 11). Per-app results vary widely, e.g. Astra's cumulative recovery ranges from 81.8% (MailHub) to 5.9% (Baserow) (p. 11).
80	5. [V] Of 977 failed atomic behaviours in full reconstruction, 59.2% were never observed in the reference. Of the rest, 1.8% were observed but not implemented, 11.1% were implemented with the wrong observable form and 27.9% produced the wrong state, route or result (p. 12).
81	6. [A] Agents' own validation (syntax checks, successful requests, selected text matches) often did not recheck the failing workflow after the last relevant edit, so mismatches went undetected (p. 12; p. 13).
82	7. [V] From depth 1 to 8, code to restore grows 9.3x and required browser actions 10.7x, but reference-observation steps per target fall from 34.60 to 8.46. Retained mask stub lines rise from 11.1% to 24.6% (p. 9; p. 10).
83	8. [V] The depth effect persists among runs with similar context lengths; e.g. in the 40–80k band, mean binary score falls from 82.6% at depth 1 to 24.2% at depth 8 (p. 39).
84	9. [V] At least one shortcut attempt (git history, public source fetch, harness probing, direct reference access) appears in 7.2% of trajectories: 19.0% for Grok 4.6, 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.3% for Astra. These channels were blocked by design (p. 10).
85	10. [V] The best model was the most observation-heavy and edit-light: Astra averages 96.3 current-app observation steps and 9.9 edit/write steps per trajectory (p. 9).
86	
87	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
88	- [A] Agents receive structured text observations, not screenshots. Visual fidelity is not evaluated and "would require criteria beyond the current replay-based behavioral checks" (p. 14).
89	- [A] Only self-contained web apps; external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop/mobile apps are future work (p. 14).
90	- [A] Benchmark coverage and quality depend on the construction model (GPT-5.6 Sol) (p. 15).
91	- [A] Results depend on the browser/agent infrastructure (replay-stable selectors, settled observations, harness), and sensitivity to these choices is uncharacterised (p. 15).
92	- [A] The isolation is not a general-purpose sandbox for hostile code (p. 24).
93	- [A] Possible misuse for cloning proprietary apps; experiments are limited to public/open-source apps (p. 15).
94	
95	## 9. Limitations we identified
96	- [I] Code quality and maintainability of the rebuilt or repaired code are not measured at all. Only behavioural replay is scored (p. 6). The full-reconstruction contract forces a single Node `handle()` entry with in-memory `context.state` (p. 37), while the originals use Django, Angular, React or Next.js with databases (p. 19). The rebuild's architecture is therefore imposed and not comparable to the original.
97	- [I] Possible self-preference and family bias:
98	  - GPT-5.6 Sol builds the traces, masks and problem statements (p. 2) and is also an evaluated model; the top model is from the same vendor (GPT-6 Astra) (p. 8).
99	  - The full-reconstruction failure analysis is done by GPT-6 Astra (p. 12), which judges its own and its competitors' failures, with no human validation reported.
100	- [I] No human check anywhere. Tasks are built "without human intervention" (p. 1), mask depth is judged by an LLM critic (p. 5), and 572 cumulative masks were merged by an LLM agent (p. 6). The only quality evidence is the replay checks and the 100% depth-1 solve rate of one model (p. 8). No sample of tasks was manually audited.
101	- [I] Oracle completeness is not measured. Unlike ProgramBench, no code coverage is reported for the trace suites. Behaviours exist only if the mining LLM found and stably replayed them; 29.5% of goals were lost (p. 7). Behaviours an agent never observes still count as failures (59.2% of failures, p. 12), but the trace bank itself may miss large parts of each app.
102	- [I] The full-reconstruction oracle checks surface identity (selectors, accessible names, labels) (p. 35), and the agent is shown the reference's selectors (p. 24). This mixes functional fidelity with DOM-level mimicry. A functionally equivalent rebuild with different labels would fail, while visual appearance is not checked at all (p. 14).
103	- [I] Contamination is not discussed. The 8 real-world apps are public GitHub projects (p. 19), so agents may partly reconstruct masked code from memory, especially for well-known clones.
104	- [I] Small and uneven samples for headline claims: one run per cell, full reconstruction on 12 apps x 3 models (36 runs) (p. 12), and per-app task pools from 2 to 372 (p. 19). Differences between close models (e.g. 45.3% vs 45.7%, p. 8) are not interpretable without variance estimates.
105	- [I] The model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) were very recent at publication and are cited to system cards (p. 16; p. 17). Results may not be reproducible once these API versions change.
106	
107	## 10. Threats to validity
108	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: no pre-mask git history, blocked egress, hidden grading files, browser-only reference access, fresh-verifier rebuild (p. 10; p. 24). [I] Remaining threats: the same model family builds and is evaluated; LLM-only task validation; memorisation of public source.
109	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 26 mostly small, self-contained CRUD-style web apps, 18 of them from one synthetic suite (OSWorld) (p. 19); a single harness; text-only observation (p. 14). Transfer to large production apps, visual-design fidelity or human-in-the-loop vibe coding is untested.
110	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Replay of mined traces is a sound behavioural oracle for the traced workflows, but it covers only discovered behaviours and also demands selector-level identity (p. 35). "Reconstruction success" therefore means reproducing specific recorded interactions, not the whole application.
111	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or tests; single runs; stratified 300-task subset. The depth trend is consistent across models and context bands (p. 39), which makes that particular finding more credible.
112	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, harness settings and pricing are reported in detail (p. 24; p. 25; p. 37). [A] The benchmark is not yet public (p. 1).
113	
114	## 11. Future research directions
115	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 14; p. 15):
116	  - add screenshots and visual-fidelity criteria;
117	  - extend to external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop and mobile apps;
118	  - study the quality–cost trade-off of the construction model;
119	  - characterise sensitivity to infrastructure choices;
120	  - use the tasks and trajectories for training (distillation, RL, curriculum by restoration depth).
121	- Suggested by us [I]:
122	  1. Measure code quality and maintainability of rebuilt apps, with a free architecture rather than a single fixed handler.
123	  2. Audit a sample of mined traces and masks by hand, and measure oracle coverage.
124	  3. Use a construction model from a different family than the evaluated models.
125	  4. Add repeated runs.
126	  5. Study a human-in-the-loop (vibe-coding) condition in which a developer steers reconstruction.
127	
128	## 12. Relevance to our research
129	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only as a documented gap).
130	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest available study of rebuilding *interactive web applications* from a running reference via its UI, which is our core scenario. It offers a reusable fidelity-testing method: deterministic replay of recorded browser workflows with expected signals and prerequisite lineages. It also gives a failure taxonomy showing that most misses come from not exploring the reference rather than from coding errors (p. 12). It shows that agents' self-validation is unreliable (p. 12). Together with ProgramBench (yang2026programbench), it shows that functional fidelity of whole-app rebuilds remains far from complete. Like ProgramBench, it does not measure the maintainability of the rebuilt code, which supports the joint fidelity-plus-quality gap in RQ5.
131	
132	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
133	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
134	|---|---|---|---|---|
135	| RQ1 | Reference-guided setting: agent interacts with a live reference web app via a browser CLI (structured text observations, no source, no screenshots) and edits a masked repo or a blank scaffold to reproduce its behaviour. | p. 3; p. 6; p. 24 | V | moderate (design fact) |
136	| RQ2 | Best full-application rebuild from a live reference recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows (12 apps); other models 21–42%. | p. 11 | V | weak (preprint, 36 single runs) |
137	| RQ2 | Partial-repair success falls as more dependent behaviours must be restored (best model 100% at depth 1 to 64% at depth 8; others to ≤32%), and the drop persists when context length is controlled. | p. 8; p. 9; p. 39 | V | weak (single runs, but consistent across 9 models) |
138	| RQ2 | Restoring UI plus logic is harder than logic alone (e.g. 92.9% vs 76.9% binary for the best model). | p. 38 | V | weak |
139	| RQ2 | 59.2% of failed behaviours in full rebuilds were never observed in the reference; 27.9% had wrong state/result and 11.1% wrong observable form. | p. 12 | V | weak (classified by an LLM that is also an evaluated model) |
140	| RQ4 | Fidelity oracle: deterministic browser-trace replay with expected signals, admitted only if replayable on the intact app, failing after masking, and passing with the gold patch. | p. 4; p. 5; p. 6 | V | moderate (design fact) |
141	| RQ4 | Agents' own validation (syntax checks, request success, partial text checks) missed behavioural mismatches with the reference. | p. 12 | A | weak |
142	| RQ4 | Tasks are built and validated without human intervention by one LLM (GPT-5.6 Sol), which is also evaluated; authors note quality depends on the construction model. | p. 1; p. 2; p. 15 | A | weak |
143	| RQ5 | Visual fidelity and screenshot-based observation are not evaluated; authors name them, plus desktop/mobile apps, as future work. Code quality of rebuilds is not measured (our observation). | p. 14 | A | weak |
144	
145	## 14. Key quotes
146	> "The distinction is thus a shift from specification consumption to specification discovery." (p. 14)
147	
148	> "the largest failure category is behavior that was not observed in the reference, accounting for 59.2% of failures" (p. 12)
149	
150	> "Similar text or element structure in observations is not sufficient." (p. 35)
151	
152	## Analyst notes
153	- Reading coverage: whole paper read, pp. 1–40, including all appendices and prompts. Figures 1, 6, 8–13 are partly garbled in the text layer, so only numbers stated in the text or tables are used. Figure 11 per-model shortcut rates were cross-checked with the text (p. 10).
154	- Uncertainties:
155	  - how the 26 and 12 apps were chosen;
156	  - whether trace suites cover most app functionality;
157	  - how much memorisation of public app source contributes.
158	  
159	  The future-dated model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash) are taken as reported; the paper is dated 16 Sep 2026, before our analysis date.
160	- Strength ratings follow research-standards §5 (preprint without replication = weak). The depth-degradation finding is the most robust internally, because it is consistent across 9 models and context bands.
161

                                             an incomplete application. We introduce ProgramDistill1 , a benchmark evaluating coding agents on features

18	# ProgramDistill: From Interactive Web Apps to Verifiable Reference-Guided SWE Tasks
19	
20	- Authors: Kim, Jeonghye; Kim, Minseon; Kim, Young Jin; Pereira, Matheus; Côté, Marc-Alexandre; Sordoni, Alessandro; Yuan, Xingdi; Shi, Zhengyan
21	- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed; v1 dated 16 Sep 2026). Affiliations: KAIST, Microsoft Research Montréal, Microsoft AI (p. 1).
22	- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.18805 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18805
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Evaluate coding agents on "reference-guided" software engineering: inferring intended behaviour by interacting with a working web application, then implementing it in an incomplete or empty application. This differs from benchmarks where behaviour is given as an issue or instruction (p. 1).
30	- [A] Turn working interactive web apps into a scalable, automatically built source of verifiable tasks ("application-to-task factorization") with controllable difficulty ("restoration depth") (p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- Not stated as formal RQs. [A] Guiding question: "Can we uncover this latent behavioral structure and use it to turn a working interactive web application into a scalable source of verifiable software-engineering tasks?" (p. 2). [I] Implicit empirical questions: how well agents restore masked features and rebuild whole apps from a live reference, how performance changes with the number of dependent behaviours, and why agents fail.
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] A fully automated LLM pipeline ("mine–craft–patch") builds tasks; two evaluation settings follow, plus trajectory and failure analyses (p. 2; p. 6).
37	- Approach / model / intervention:
38	  - [V] *Mine*: LLM agents (Planner, Collector, Relabeler, Reflector), with read access to the source and the live app, propose behaviour goals, drive the app through a Playwright browser helper, and record replayable traces of actions plus expected observable signals (accessible names, visible text, URL, state). A trace is admitted only if it replays deterministically from a reset state (p. 3; p. 4; p. 25).
39	  - [V] *Craft*: an LLM masks (deletes) the source implementing a behaviour, either logic only or logic plus UI. A mask is accepted only if the app still builds, prerequisite traces still pass, the target trace fails, and an LLM "mask-depth critic" judges the deletion substantive. Masks along a prerequisite lineage are combined into cumulative tasks, and the reversed mask is the gold patch, which must replay the whole lineage (p. 4; p. 5; p. 6).
40	  - [V] *Patch*, partial-application reconstruction: the agent gets the masked repository, an LLM-written behavioural problem statement, and browser access to the live reference (no reference source, no internet) (p. 6).
41	  - [V] *Patch*, full-application reconstruction: the agent starts from a minimal scaffold plus a product-level capability description and must rebuild the whole app from the live reference (p. 6; p. 10; p. 11).
42	  - [V] All construction stages use GPT-5.6 Sol (p. 2; p. 7).
43	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 9 frontier models compared on partial reconstruction; 3 models (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) on full reconstruction. Logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks; restoration depths 1–8 (p. 8; p. 11). No human or non-agent baseline.
44	- [I] Relation to our topic: full-application reconstruction is very close to our scenario of rebuilding a web application by observing its UI and behaviour, with no access to its source. Partial reconstruction resembles restoring missing features in an existing codebase by consulting a working product.
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] 26 self-contained web apps: 18 adapted from the OSWorld web-application suite and 8 real-world open-source projects or SaaS clones (Actual Budget, Reactive Resume, Baserow, two Trello clones, two Jira clones, a Calendly clone), using Django, Angular, React and Next.js with SQL and document back ends. Each is pinned to a commit (p. 19).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit:
49	  - [V] Mining: 2,800 candidate goals, 2,350 collected, 2,165 reproduced and 1,975 verified behaviours; maximum lineage depth 17 (mean 3.40) (p. 7).
50	  - [V] Tasks: 4,063 in total, 2,862 atomic and 1,201 cumulative; 1,997 logic-only and 2,066 logic-and-UI (p. 7).
51	  - [V] Per-app task counts are very uneven, from 2 (ExpenseFlow) to 372 (Reactive Resume) (p. 19).
52	  - [V] Evaluation suite ProgramDistill-300: 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks covering 269 lineages and all 26 apps (p. 8).
53	  - [V] Full reconstruction: 12 apps, 590 atomic and 413 cumulative behaviour tests, 36 runs (p. 11; p. 12).
54	- Sampling / selection method: [V] ProgramDistill-300 is stratified by restoration depth (quotas 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, 25 for depths 1–8) and selected round-robin across apps (p. 8). [I] Why these 26 apps, and why these 12 for full reconstruction ("twelve stateful web applications", p. 11), is not explained beyond "complementary sources" (p. 3).
55	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We are working on a public release of the ProgramDistill benchmark" (p. 1). Not yet released at time of writing; prompts are given in the appendix (p. 25; p. 30; p. 33).
56	
57	## 5. Experimental setup
58	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Modified R2E-Gym harness with tools `execute_bash`, `file_editor`, `search` and `finish`. A browser CLI drives both the reference and the current app (p. 8). Agents see only structured text observations (visible text, element IDs, roles, accessible names, input values); full reconstruction additionally exposes selectors. Screenshots and raw HTML are excluded (p. 3; p. 24).
59	- [V] Partial reconstruction: reasoning effort high, at most 1,000 steps, 150k-token history cutoff. Full reconstruction: reasoning effort max, at most 10,000 steps, 500k-token cutoff. Per-tool timeout 90 s, no aggregate time limit (p. 24).
60	- [V] Determinism: application state is reset before each collection and replay, and a shared fake clock (libfaketime plus a browser Date offset) is used (p. 3; p. 19; p. 20).
61	- [V] Isolation: the reference is reachable only via the browser helper, public egress is blocked, there is no pre-mask git history, and grading traces are private. Submissions are rebuilt and replayed in a fresh verifier (p. 10; p. 23; p. 24).
62	- [V] The full-reconstruction scaffold requires an `app.js` exporting `async function handle(req, res, context)`, with state kept in `context.state` (p. 37).
63	- [V] Number of runs: one per model and task (partial) and one per model and app (36 full-reconstruction runs, p. 12). Repeats or seeds: not reported.
64	- [V] Cost: tokens x LiteLLM list prices (p. 37). One GPT-6 Astra pass over 300 tasks took about 557 minutes on 4 servers (p. 37).
65	- Code availability: [A] release in progress (p. 1).
66	
67	## 6. Evaluation metrics
68	- Replay verifier V(A, L): returns 1 only if every recorded browser action completes and every expected signal is satisfied, replaying the whole prerequisite lineage without LLM involvement (p. 4).
69	- Binary score: 1 only if the complete lineage passes after the agent's patch. Chain score: fraction of repair targets passed, giving partial credit (p. 6).
70	- Full reconstruction: atomic behaviour recovery (fraction of single-behaviour tests passed, with prerequisites replayed) and cumulative workflow recovery (binary and chain) (p. 6; p. 11).
71	- [V] Source-level matching is not required: function names, variables and structure may differ if behaviour replays (p. 6). [V] In full reconstruction, however, selectors and accessible names must match the reference, because evaluation "replays user interactions using selectors" (p. 35).
72	- Diagnostics: interaction counts (observation, read/search, edit/write steps), share of unchanged target files and retained stub lines, shortcut-attempt rate, failure categories (p. 9; p. 10; p. 12).
73	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; means only. Pearson correlations between prompt size and binary score are reported in the context-length check (p. 40).
74	
75	## 7. Key findings
76	1. [V] Partial reconstruction (ProgramDistill-300): mean binary score is 84.3% for GPT-6 Astra, 68.7% for Claude Opus 5 and 60.7% for GPT-5.6 Sol, with a middle tier at 45.3–48.3% and Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview lowest at 22.3%. Mean cost per trajectory is $33.99, $28.86 and $16.01 for the top three (p. 8; p. 38).
77	2. [V] Success drops with restoration depth: Astra falls from 100% at depth 1 to 64.0% at depth 8, Opus 5 from 96% to 32.0% and Sol from 92% to 32.0%; every other model keeps less than half of its depth-1 performance (p. 8; p. 9).
78	3. [V] Restoring UI as well as logic is harder. Binary scores for logic-only vs logic-and-UI masks are 92.9% vs 76.9% for Astra and 76.4% vs 46.9% for Sol (p. 38).
79	4. [V] Full-application reconstruction (12 apps): Astra recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows, Opus 5 42.03% and 28.81%, and Sol 33.39% and 21.07% (p. 11). Per-app results vary widely, e.g. Astra's cumulative recovery ranges from 81.8% (MailHub) to 5.9% (Baserow) (p. 11).
80	5. [V] Of 977 failed atomic behaviours in full reconstruction, 59.2% were never observed in the reference. Of the rest, 1.8% were observed but not implemented, 11.1% were implemented with the wrong observable form and 27.9% produced the wrong state, route or result (p. 12).
81	6. [A] Agents' own validation (syntax checks, successful requests, selected text matches) often did not recheck the failing workflow after the last relevant edit, so mismatches went undetected (p. 12; p. 13).
82	7. [V] From depth 1 to 8, code to restore grows 9.3x and required browser actions 10.7x, but reference-observation steps per target fall from 34.60 to 8.46. Retained mask stub lines rise from 11.1% to 24.6% (p. 9; p. 10).
83	8. [V] The depth effect persists among runs with similar context lengths; e.g. in the 40–80k band, mean binary score falls from 82.6% at depth 1 to 24.2% at depth 8 (p. 39).
84	9. [V] At least one shortcut attempt (git history, public source fetch, harness probing, direct reference access) appears in 7.2% of trajectories: 19.0% for Grok 4.6, 17.7% for Gemini 3.1 Pro and 0.3% for Astra. These channels were blocked by design (p. 10).
85	10. [V] The best model was the most observation-heavy and edit-light: Astra averages 96.3 current-app observation steps and 9.9 edit/write steps per trajectory (p. 9).
86	
87	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
88	- [A] Agents receive structured text observations, not screenshots. Visual fidelity is not evaluated and "would require criteria beyond the current replay-based behavioral checks" (p. 14).
89	- [A] Only self-contained web apps; external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop/mobile apps are future work (p. 14).
90	- [A] Benchmark coverage and quality depend on the construction model (GPT-5.6 Sol) (p. 15).
91	- [A] Results depend on the browser/agent infrastructure (replay-stable selectors, settled observations, harness), and sensitivity to these choices is uncharacterised (p. 15).
92	- [A] The isolation is not a general-purpose sandbox for hostile code (p. 24).
93	- [A] Possible misuse for cloning proprietary apps; experiments are limited to public/open-source apps (p. 15).
94	
95	## 9. Limitations we identified
96	- [I] Code quality and maintainability of the rebuilt or repaired code are not measured at all. Only behavioural replay is scored (p. 6). The full-reconstruction contract forces a single Node `handle()` entry with in-memory `context.state` (p. 37), while the originals use Django, Angular, React or Next.js with databases (p. 19). The rebuild's architecture is therefore imposed and not comparable to the original.
97	- [I] Possible self-preference and family bias:
98	  - GPT-5.6 Sol builds the traces, masks and problem statements (p. 2) and is also an evaluated model; the top model is from the same vendor (GPT-6 Astra) (p. 8).
99	  - The full-reconstruction failure analysis is done by GPT-6 Astra (p. 12), which judges its own and its competitors' failures, with no human validation reported.
100	- [I] No human check anywhere. Tasks are built "without human intervention" (p. 1), mask depth is judged by an LLM critic (p. 5), and 572 cumulative masks were merged by an LLM agent (p. 6). The only quality evidence is the replay checks and the 100% depth-1 solve rate of one model (p. 8). No sample of tasks was manually audited.
101	- [I] Oracle completeness is not measured. Unlike ProgramBench, no code coverage is reported for the trace suites. Behaviours exist only if the mining LLM found and stably replayed them; 29.5% of goals were lost (p. 7). Behaviours an agent never observes still count as failures (59.2% of failures, p. 12), but the trace bank itself may miss large parts of each app.
102	- [I] The full-reconstruction oracle checks surface identity (selectors, accessible names, labels) (p. 35), and the agent is shown the reference's selectors (p. 24). This mixes functional fidelity with DOM-level mimicry. A functionally equivalent rebuild with different labels would fail, while visual appearance is not checked at all (p. 14).
103	- [I] Contamination is not discussed. The 8 real-world apps are public GitHub projects (p. 19), so agents may partly reconstruct masked code from memory, especially for well-known clones.
104	- [I] Small and uneven samples for headline claims: one run per cell, full reconstruction on 12 apps x 3 models (36 runs) (p. 12), and per-app task pools from 2 to 372 (p. 19). Differences between close models (e.g. 45.3% vs 45.7%, p. 8) are not interpretable without variance estimates.
105	- [I] The model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol) were very recent at publication and are cited to system cards (p. 16; p. 17). Results may not be reproducible once these API versions change.
106	
107	## 10. Threats to validity
108	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [V] Leakage controls: no pre-mask git history, blocked egress, hidden grading files, browser-only reference access, fresh-verifier rebuild (p. 10; p. 24). [I] Remaining threats: the same model family builds and is evaluated; LLM-only task validation; memorisation of public source.
109	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 26 mostly small, self-contained CRUD-style web apps, 18 of them from one synthetic suite (OSWorld) (p. 19); a single harness; text-only observation (p. 14). Transfer to large production apps, visual-design fidelity or human-in-the-loop vibe coding is untested.
110	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] Replay of mined traces is a sound behavioural oracle for the traced workflows, but it covers only discovered behaviours and also demands selector-level identity (p. 35). "Reconstruction success" therefore means reproducing specific recorded interactions, not the whole application.
111	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No CIs or tests; single runs; stratified 300-task subset. The depth trend is consistent across models and context bands (p. 39), which makes that particular finding more credible.
112	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts, harness settings and pricing are reported in detail (p. 24; p. 25; p. 37). [A] The benchmark is not yet public (p. 1).
113	
114	## 11. Future research directions
115	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 14; p. 15):
116	  - add screenshots and visual-fidelity criteria;
117	  - extend to external services, nondeterministic state, and desktop and mobile apps;
118	  - study the quality–cost trade-off of the construction model;
119	  - characterise sensitivity to infrastructure choices;
120	  - use the tasks and trajectories for training (distillation, RL, curriculum by restoration depth).
121	- Suggested by us [I]:
122	  1. Measure code quality and maintainability of rebuilt apps, with a free architecture rather than a single fixed handler.
123	  2. Audit a sample of mined traces and masks by hand, and measure oracle coverage.
124	  3. Use a construction model from a different family than the evaluated models.
125	  4. Add repeated runs.
126	  5. Study a human-in-the-loop (vibe-coding) condition in which a developer steers reconstruction.
127	
128	## 12. Relevance to our research
129	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only as a documented gap).
130	- How it informs our work [I]: This is the closest available study of rebuilding *interactive web applications* from a running reference via its UI, which is our core scenario. It offers a reusable fidelity-testing method: deterministic replay of recorded browser workflows with expected signals and prerequisite lineages. It also gives a failure taxonomy showing that most misses come from not exploring the reference rather than from coding errors (p. 12). It shows that agents' self-validation is unreliable (p. 12). Together with ProgramBench (yang2026programbench), it shows that functional fidelity of whole-app rebuilds remains far from complete. Like ProgramBench, it does not measure the maintainability of the rebuilt code, which supports the joint fidelity-plus-quality gap in RQ5.
131	
132	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
133	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
134	|---|---|---|---|---|
135	| RQ1 | Reference-guided setting: agent interacts with a live reference web app via a browser CLI (structured text observations, no source, no screenshots) and edits a masked repo or a blank scaffold to reproduce its behaviour. | p. 3; p. 6; p. 24 | V | moderate (design fact) |
136	| RQ2 | Best full-application rebuild from a live reference recovers 58.98% of atomic behaviours and 49.15% of cumulative workflows (12 apps); other models 21–42%. | p. 11 | V | weak (preprint, 36 single runs) |
137	| RQ2 | Partial-repair success falls as more dependent behaviours must be restored (best model 100% at depth 1 to 64% at depth 8; others to ≤32%), and the drop persists when context length is controlled. | p. 8; p. 9; p. 39 | V | weak (single runs, but consistent across 9 models) |
138	| RQ2 | Restoring UI plus logic is harder than logic alone (e.g. 92.9% vs 76.9% binary for the best model). | p. 38 | V | weak |
139	| RQ2 | 59.2% of failed behaviours in full rebuilds were never observed in the reference; 27.9% had wrong state/result and 11.1% wrong observable form. | p. 12 | V | weak (classified by an LLM that is also an evaluated model) |
140	| RQ4 | Fidelity oracle: deterministic browser-trace replay with expected signals, admitted only if replayable on the intact app, failing after masking, and passing with the gold patch. | p. 4; p. 5; p. 6 | V | moderate (design fact) |
141	| RQ4 | Agents' own validation (syntax checks, request success, partial text checks) missed behavioural mismatches with the reference. | p. 12 | A | weak |
142	| RQ4 | Tasks are built and validated without human intervention by one LLM (GPT-5.6 Sol), which is also evaluated; authors note quality depends on the construction model. | p. 1; p. 2; p. 15 | A | weak |
143	| RQ5 | Visual fidelity and screenshot-based observation are not evaluated; authors name them, plus desktop/mobile apps, as future work. Code quality of rebuilds is not measured (our observation). | p. 14 | A | weak |
144	
145	## 14. Key quotes
146	> "The distinction is thus a shift from specification consumption to specification discovery." (p. 14)
147	
148	> "the largest failure category is behavior that was not observed in the reference, accounting for 59.2% of failures" (p. 12)
149	
150	> "Similar text or element structure in observations is not sufficient." (p. 35)
151	
152	## Analyst notes
153	- Reading coverage: whole paper read, pp. 1–40, including all appendices and prompts. Figures 1, 6, 8–13 are partly garbled in the text layer, so only numbers stated in the text or tables are used. Figure 11 per-model shortcut rates were cross-checked with the text (p. 10).
154	- Uncertainties:
155	  - how the 26 and 12 apps were chosen;
156	  - whether trace suites cover most app functionality;
157	  - how much memorisation of public app source contributes.
158	  
159	  The future-dated model names (GPT-6 Astra, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.7 Flash) are taken as reported; the paper is dated 16 Sep 2026, before our analysis date.
160	- Strength ratings follow research-standards §5 (preprint without replication = weak). The depth-degradation finding is the most robust internally, because it is consistent across 9 models and context bands.

ProgramDistill: From Interactive Web Apps to Verifiable Reference-Guided SWE Tasks



  ProgramDistill-300.      Evaluating all 4,063 tasks for every model would be prohibitively expensive, so we define a
  fixed 300-task evaluation suite. We stratify tasks by restoration depth rL using quotas of 50, 45, 45, 40, 35, 30, 30, and
  25 for depths 1 through 8. Within each depth, tasks are selected round-robin across applications to preserve coverage of
  all 26 apps and prevent applications with larger task pools from dominating. The resulting suite covers 269 distinct
  lineages and contains 50 atomic and 250 cumulative tasks, with 140 logic-only and 160 logic-and-UI masks.

  3.2                            Partial-Application Reconstruction

  We evaluate nine frontier models—GPT-6 Astra [24], GPT-5.6 Sol [23], Claude Opus 5 [3], Claude Sonnet 5 [4],
  Gemini 3.7 Flash [9], Gemini 3.6 Flash [8], Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview [7], Grok 4.6 [30] and GPT-5.3 Codex [22]—on
  ProgramDistill-300, with reasoning effort set to high. Each model receives a masked application and a problem
  statement and must recover the missing behavior by inspecting a reference, editing the current implementation, and
  validating its changes against the live application. Depth-1 tasks are atomic repairs, while depths 2 through 8 combine
  multiple repair targets from a prerequisite lineage.
  Agent harness.     All models use the same modified R2E-Gym [14] agent harness. The harness exposes four coding
  tools: execute_bash, file_editor, search, and finish. Through execute_bash, the agent can also invoke the
  browser CLI to observe and interact with both the masked current application and the working reference. Appendix C
  describes the harness design and execution settings.

  3.2.1                            Model Performance Comparison
  We evaluate nine models on ProgramDistill-300, comparing repair performance with model cost. Figure 7(a) plots
  mean binary score against mean trajectory cost in USD, while Appendix H.2 reports the corresponding chain-score
  results. GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest mean binary score at 84.3%, followed by Claude Opus 5 at 68.7% and
  GPT-5.6 Sol at 60.7%. Their mean trajectory costs are $33.99, $28.86, and $16.01, respectively. Astra gains 15.7
  percentage points over Opus 5 at about 18% higher mean trajectory cost. Grok 4.6, Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.3 Codex,
  and Gemini 3.7 Flash form a middle tier, with scores between 45.3% and 48.3%.
  Higher expenditure does not always yield better repair performance. Gemini 3.7 Flash nearly matches GPT-5.3 Codex
  (45.3% vs. 45.7%) at a mean trajectory cost of $3.89 versus $5.99, while Grok 4.6 slightly exceeds Claude Sonnet 5
  (48.3% vs. 47.3%) at $8.83 versus $13.12 per trajectory.
  Mask scope provides a complementary view of repair difficulty. Astra’s chain score is 96.2% on logic-only tasks and
  84.9% on logic-and-UI tasks. The 11.3-point gap shows that interface reconstruction remains harder even when partial
  restoration receives credit. Appendix H.1 reports the full scope comparison.

                                                                                               Astra


  Astra achieves 92.9% binary success on logic-only tasks and 76.9% on logic-and-UI tasks, a 16.0-point gap. The chain
  score gives partial credit for behaviors recovered before the first failure in a cumulative task. Under this metric, Astra
  achieves 96.2% on logic-only tasks and 84.9% on logic-and-UI tasks, a 11.3-point gap. The scope comparison therefore
  captures both complete task success and the extent of partial restoration.

much larger volume of browser feedback, Opus 5 still recovers fewer behaviors than Astra, suggesting that observation

3.3.2       Analysis
Full-application reconstruction remains difficult even for the strongest agents. We therefore ask why agents fail to
recover behaviors that are available to inspect in a working reference. We analyze 977 failed atomic behaviors across
the 36 reconstruction runs in Table 1, using the submitted source, and recorded reference and current observations
with GPT-6 Astra. Each failure is assigned to one of four categories: not observed, observed but not implemented,
implemented with the wrong observable form, or implemented with the wrong state, route, or result. We also examine
why the agent’s own validation did not expose and correct the remaining difference.

Observed, not implemented            18 (1.8%)

     Wrong observable form                108 (11.1%)

         Wrong state or result                       273 (27.9%)                                  Sol (n = 393)                 64.6%                        20.9%    14.2%

Figure 12: Full-application reconstruction failures. Across 36 runs on 12 applications, (a) counts failures in the four
categories and (b) shows their distribution within each model’s failures.

Behavior-level reconstruction outcomes. As shown in Figure 12, the largest failure category is behavior that
was not observed in the reference, accounting for 59.2% of failures. The remaining failures occur after the relevant
behavior has been observed. Of these, 1.8% are observed but not implemented, 11.1% are implemented with the
wrong observable form, and 27.9% produce the wrong state, route, or result. These outcomes reveal difficulties both in
exploring the reference and in faithfully reproducing behaviors that have already been observed.

What validation missed.          Agents checked that their reconstructed applications worked, but these checks did not
always establish faithful reproduction of the reference behavior. In the failure cases in Figure 13, agents often validated
related functionality or a limited set of workflows without rechecking the failing workflow after the final relevant source
edit. For example, validating native resume creation and export did not reveal a failure in external JSON Resume import,
while syntax-only checks did not reveal that report edits in W&B were not persisted.
