1	---
2	key: mock2026vibe
3	status: ready
4	evidence_basis: full-text
5	design: pre-experimental static-group comparison (solo vs collaborative TDD with professionals) plus exploratory repeated runs of fully-automated and agentic workflows
6	dataset: 2 small Python TDD tasks (TextFormatter string centring); baseline test suite of 12 assertions derived by category-partition testing
7	sample_size: 16 professionals (9 solo, 7 collaborative); 3 fully-automated runs; 12 agentic runs (MetaGPT X, GPT-5 / Claude Sonnet 4)
8	metrics: test pass rate on baseline tests, McCabe complexity, statement/branch coverage, LCS/Levenshtein similarity, test methods/assertions, iterations, time
9	main_finding: Agentic runs passed most baseline tests (mean 94.6%) fastest but with higher complexity and lower coverage; collaborative vibe coding did not beat solo coding.
10	relevance: medium
11	analysed: 2026-11-11
12	---
13	<!-- Frontmatter: single-line values; they feed literature-matrix.md via `rlab index`.
14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.
16	     relevance: high | medium | low. -->
17	
18	# Vibe Coding: An experiment with test-driven development
19	
20	- Authors: Mock, Moritz; Russo, Barbara
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Empirical Software Engineering (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1007/s10664-026-10950-z · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10950-z
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	Note on the source: our PDF is the Springer open-access version (Empirical Software Engineering (2027) 32:40, accepted 4 August 2026; 48 pages). Metadata gives year 2026 (online publication); the printed volume year is 2027 (p. 1).
29	
30	## 1. Research objective
31	- [A] To investigate how humans and conversational LLMs (CLLMs) can collaborate "as peers through vibe coding", by comparing four interaction models (solo, collaborative, fully automated, agentic) within a Test-Driven Development (TDD) process (p. 1, p. 2).
32	- [V] Empirical goal (GQM): "Analyse code generation to compare human-CLLM interaction models with respect to code quality and development process efficiency, from the viewpoint of developers, in the context of TDD" (p. 11).
33	- [I] Important for our use: in this paper "vibe coding" means the collaborative model in which the human writes TDD tests and the CLLM writes production code through fixed, scripted prompts that participants could not modify (p. 7, p. 8, p. 15). This is narrower and more structured than the "minimal review" vibe coding of grey-literature definitions (e.g. fawzy2026vibe).
34	
35	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
36	- [V] RQ1: How does the quality of production code vary across interaction models? Sub-questions: RQ1.1 syntactic similarity, RQ1.2 functional correctness, RQ1.3 complexity (p. 11, p. 12).
37	- [V] RQ2: How does the quality of the tests vary? RQ2.1 structural complexity of tests, RQ2.2 coverage (p. 13).
38	- [V] RQ3: How does TDD process efficiency vary? (p. 13)
39	- [V] Statistical null hypotheses per pairwise comparison are one-tailed (H0: A <= B, per Tables 9-13) (p. 25, p. 27); no substantive directional hypotheses stated up front.
40	
41	## 3. Methodology
42	- Research design: [V] Two complementary settings: (i) a "controlled pre-experimental study" using a Static-Group Comparison design with a control group (solo-coding, CG) and an experimental group (collaborative, EG) of professionals; (ii) "repeated exploratory executions" of fully-automated and agentic workflows on the same tasks (p. 1, p. 14, p. 15). A *pre-experimental design* is a weak experimental design (Campbell & Stanley) without pre-tests and, in the classical form, without random assignment.
43	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Four interaction models operationalised as workflows (p. 7, p. 8): solo-coding (human only); collaborative (human writes tests, CLLM generates production code; this is what the paper calls vibe coding); fully-automated (scripts drive a single CLLM to write both tests and code); agentic (MetaGPT X platform, Engineer mode) (p. 7, p. 8, p. 17). Prompts built from White et al.'s prompt-pattern catalogue (Game Play, Persona, Template, Context Manager, Question Refinement) (p. 8); prompts tell the CLLM "Built-in functions are not allowed" (Table 7, p. 20). A failing test triggers up to five automatic re-prompts before control returns to the human (p. 19). Each iteration is a new session (p. 22).
44	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Solo-coding (human-only TDD) is the control condition (p. 15). A baseline test suite derived from the specification by category-partition testing is the correctness oracle (p. 11, p. 12).
45	
46	## 4. Dataset and sample
47	- Data source(s): [V] Two development tasks of a Python `TextFormatter` class: centre one word in a line (task 1) and centre two words (task 2), plus a `setLineWidth` setter (Fig. 4, p. 12). Baseline suite: two test methods with 5 and 7 assertions (p. 12, p. 28).
48	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 16 professional developers: 9 solo-coding (P1-P9), 7 collaborative (P10-P16) (p. 16). 5 came from a preliminary experiment (Mock et al. 2025), extended with 11 more (p. 13). Fully-automated: 3 runs (FA1-FA3) (p. 42). Agentic: 12 runs = 2 models (ChatGPT 5, Claude Sonnet 4) x 2 prompt scenarios x 3 runs (p. 42).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] IT professionals from Italy, Denmark and Brazil with TDD and Python experience (p. 15). Recruitment method: not reported beyond this. The authors justify N by the "typical" 15-25 range for studies with professionals (p. 13, p. 15). Participants "randomly assigned" to groups (p. 15). Experience was uneven: many participants had <1 year TDD and/or <1 year Python (Table 5, p. 16). No power analysis reported.
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] Toolbox, participant data and questionnaire responses in a GitHub replication package, https://github.com/moritzmock/AI4TDD_journal (p. 43, p. 45). We did not open it.
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Google Colab environment; sessions remote (screen sharing) or in person; 40-minute limit; internet search allowed but not full solutions or independent CLLM use, monitored by observation (p. 15). Collaborative participants could not modify prompts (p. 15). Collaborative and fully-automated workflows used OpenAI GPT-3.5 Turbo via API (p. 14, p. 17). Agentic workflow used MetaGPT X web interface with ChatGPT 5 or Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). Agentic runs pooled across models and prompts after observing "little difference" (p. 17). Time self-reported by humans, measured by runtime (`time` command) for automated workflows (p. 13, p. 17). Iterations not collectable for agentic runs (p. 17). Temperature or other model parameters: not reported. Model version dates/snapshots: not reported.
54	- Code availability: [V] Toolbox and data in the GitHub replication package (p. 43).
55	
56	## 6. Evaluation metrics
57	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen: [V] (Table 4, p. 14)
58	  - TPR (Test Pass Rate): share of baseline tests passing on the production code — functional correctness, ISO 25010 sub-attribute (p. 11, p. 12, p. 14).
59	  - MCC (McCabe complexity), SCB/BCB (statement/branch coverage of the production code by the baseline tests) — structural complexity as a maintainability-related attribute (p. 12, p. 14).
60	  - LCS (longest common subsequence) and LED (Levenshtein edit distance) — syntactic similarity between workflows' code (p. 11, p. 14).
61	  - TM (test methods), TAM (assertions per method), SC/BC (coverage of own code by own tests) — test quality (p. 13, p. 14).
62	  - Number of iterations and Time — process efficiency (p. 13, p. 14). CLOC/TLOC reported for size (p. 13).
63	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] Kruskal-Wallis H with epsilon-squared effect size as a screen; one-tailed Mann-Whitney U pairwise with Cliff's delta; alpha = 0.05; Holm-Bonferroni correction over six pairwise comparisons per metric (p. 10, p. 11). Confidence intervals: not reported. Means and SDs per group in Table 16 (p. 41, p. 42).
64	
65	## 7. Key findings
66	1. [V] Kruskal-Wallis significant for CLOC, TPR, MCC, BCB, SC, BC and Time; large effects for CLOC (0.34), TPR (0.52), MCC (0.5), Time (0.63) (Table 8, p. 23).
67	2. [V] Functional correctness (TPR): agentic mean 94.58% vs solo 62.0%, collaborative 60.8%, fully-automated 83.3% (Table 16, p. 41, p. 42). Agentic beats every other workflow after Holm-Bonferroni (e.g. agentic > solo: U = 106.5, Cliff's delta 0.97, p = 7.81e-05) (Table 9, p. 25).
68	3. [V] Collaborative (the paper's vibe coding) vs solo-coding: no significant difference in TPR (U = 36.5, delta -0.16, p = 0.314) or MCC (p = 0.479) (Table 9, p. 25; Table 10, p. 27). TPR within humans ranged widely: 8.3% (P7) to 100% (P13); SD 27.3 (solo) and 36.8 (collaborative) (p. 26, p. 41).
69	4. [V] Agentic code is more complex: MCC mean 11.67 vs 6.44 (solo), 6.57 (collaborative), 6.0 (fully-automated) (p. 41, p. 42); significant after correction vs all three (Table 10, p. 27). Baseline branch coverage lower for agentic (mean 65.33%) than solo (83.89%) and collaborative (79.00%) (p. 41, p. 42; Table 10, p. 27).
70	5. [A] The authors interpret the uncovered branches as agent "implementation decisions that are not explicitly defined by the functional specifications", making agentic solutions "architecturally more complex and potentially more difficult to maintain" (p. 35). Not directly measured.
71	6. [V] Agentic code "preserves the main implementation but adds helper methods, logging, and validation"; agentic code shares long common subsequences with other workflows but has larger local edit distance (p. 24).
72	7. [V] Test quality: fully-automated tests always one assertion per method, three methods (p. 28); agentic tests had lower statement and branch coverage than solo tests (SC: U = 88.5, delta -0.64, p = 6.42e-03; BC: p = 7.31e-03), significant after correction (Table 12, p. 30; p. 31). Collaborative test organisation closest to the baseline suite (qualitative) (p. 28).
73	8. [V] Efficiency: agentic fastest (mean 75 s) vs fully-automated 800 s, collaborative 2,057 s, solo 2,266 s (p. 41, p. 42); collaborative participants averaged 12.1 iterations, 5.6 of them needing assertion rework (Table 14, p. 33).
74	9. [A] Choice of interaction model should depend on the objective: agentic for speed and production-code correctness, human-involved workflows for test quality and control (p. 40).
75	
76	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
77	- [A] Human and autonomous workflows were evaluated in different settings (controlled experiment vs repeated executions); comparisons across them need care (p. 36).
78	- [A] Results may be affected by participants' TDD and Python experience (p. 36).
79	- [A] Limited number of professionals reduces statistical power; increasing N was not feasible (p. 13, p. 36).
80	- [A] Instrumentation, baseline test suite, model configuration, TDD process and environment may have influenced the data; not addressed exhaustively (p. 37).
81	- [A] Tasks are simple (p. 37). A single CLLM (ChatGPT via API) for the human-involved workflows (p. 37).
82	- [A] Participants could have used an AI tool on a second screen; cannot be fully ruled out (p. 15).
83	- [A] The agentic part "should be considered exploratory" (p. 17).
84	
85	## 9. Limitations we identified
86	- [I] Model confound: collaborative and fully-automated workflows used GPT-3.5 Turbo (p. 14, p. 17), while agentic runs used ChatGPT 5 and Claude Sonnet 4 (p. 17). The agentic advantage in TPR and time cannot be separated from the large model-generation gap. The authors call ChatGPT 5 "the most similar" model (p. 17), which we find hard to accept. This undermines the cross-workflow comparison that drives the main conclusions.
87	- [I] Very small groups: 9 vs 7 humans (p. 16), 3 fully-automated runs (p. 42). Repeated runs of the same configuration are not independent participants, yet they enter the same Mann-Whitney tests as people. With n = 3 (fully-automated) the minimum attainable one-tailed p-value is limited, so non-significance there is uninformative.
88	- [I] Design inconsistency: a Static-Group Comparison is, by definition, a design without randomisation, yet participants are said to be "randomly assigned" (p. 14, p. 15); 5 of the 16 came from an earlier preliminary session (p. 13), so session is a possible confound. No pre-test of skill; groups differ in experience (Table 5, p. 16).
89	- [I] Time is self-reported by humans (rounded to minutes, values like 2,400 s) but machine-measured for automated runs (p. 13, p. 41). Differences in Time mix measurement methods.
90	- [I] Two tiny string-formatting tasks with a 12-assertion oracle (p. 12) say little about application-level generation. TPR is assertion-level (e.g. 8.3% = 1/12).
91	- [I] The paper's "vibe coding" condition forbids prompt modification (p. 15) and uses scripted prompts, so it does not represent free-form vibe coding. Conclusions about "vibe coding" should be read as conclusions about this structured TDD workflow.
92	- [I] Some claims go beyond the data: the claim that humans "can reach the same level of correctness in collaborative settings" (p. 26) rests on single participants (P13: 100%) while the collaborative mean is 60.8% (p. 41). The Related Work states "the agentic workflow statistically produces higher-quality code" (p. 40), which conflicts with the higher complexity and lower coverage reported (p. 27, p. 35).
93	- [I] MCC is the only maintainability proxy; no code smells, readability or static-analysis measures.
94	
95	## 10. Threats to validity
96	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Model generation confounded with workflow (see section 9); session (preliminary vs main) and experience imbalance; self-reported vs measured time. [A] Possible hidden AI use (p. 15).
97	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Simple tasks, single CLLM for human workflows (p. 37). [I] Python-only, function-level tasks, one agentic platform; results do not transfer to multi-file applications or UI work.
98	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TPR against a 12-assertion spec-derived suite is a reasonable small-scale functional-correctness oracle; MCC alone is a thin proxy for maintainability; lower baseline coverage of agentic code partly reflects added validation/logging rather than lower quality.
99	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Holm-Bonferroni correction and effect sizes reported (p. 10, p. 11). [A] Low power acknowledged (p. 36). [I] Non-independent repeated runs pooled as samples; no confidence intervals; one-tailed tests chosen for every direction.
100	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts (Table 7, p. 20), metrics definitions (p. 14), per-participant data (p. 41, p. 42) and GitHub package (p. 43). [I] Agentic runs via a web interface of a commercial platform are hard to reproduce; model parameters not reported.
101	
102	## 11. Future research directions
103	- Stated by authors [A]: extend to other development practices, CLLMs and agentic platforms (p. 40); investigate whether phase-based and iterative process models remain appropriate when AI can generate complete solutions (p. 40); apply the fully-automated evaluation suite to MBPP and HumanEval (p. 40); study agentic performance under different prompting settings (p. 17); more integrated experimental platforms than Colab (p. 34).
104	- Suggested by us [I]: hold the model constant across workflows; use larger, application-level tasks; measure maintainability with more than MCC (e.g. static-analysis smells, change effort); for our project, reuse the idea of a specification-derived oracle test suite (category-partition) as a functional-fidelity measure for a reconstructed app.
105	
106	## 12. Relevance to our research
107	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (contrasts structured vibe coding with agentic generation), RQ2 (functional correctness measured by a spec-derived baseline test suite), RQ3 (complexity and coverage of AI-generated vs human code), RQ4 (design weaknesses: tiny N, model confound, mixed measurement), RQ5 (no application-level or maintainability-focused evaluation).
108	- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few peer-reviewed controlled experiments that labels its condition "vibe coding" and compares it with human-only and agentic generation. Its evaluation framework (oracle tests for correctness + complexity/coverage for internal quality + time/iterations for effort) is a template our study design could scale up. Its findings are function-level and confounded, so they should not be used as evidence about application reconstruction. Relevance medium for RQ4/RQ5 design lessons, low for direct outcome evidence.
109	
110	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
111	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
112	|---|---|---|---|---|
113	| RQ1 | "Vibe coding" operationalised as human-written TDD tests plus CLLM-generated code via fixed scripted prompts; agentic coding via MetaGPT X as the autonomous contrast | p. 7, p. 8, p. 15, p. 17 | V | moderate |
114	| RQ2 | Agentic runs passed more spec-derived baseline tests (mean TPR 94.58%) than solo (62.0%), collaborative (60.8%) and fully-automated (83.3%) workflows; significant after Holm-Bonferroni, but agentic used newer models (GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4 vs GPT-3.5 Turbo) | p. 25, p. 41, p. 42 | V | weak |
115	| RQ2 | Collaborative vibe coding did not differ significantly from solo human coding in functional correctness (TPR p = 0.314); human results varied from 8.3% to 100% | p. 25, p. 41 | V | weak |
116	| RQ3 | Agentic code had higher McCabe complexity (mean 11.67 vs about 6-6.6 for other workflows) and lower baseline branch coverage (65.3% vs 79-84% for human workflows), adding helpers, logging and validation | p. 24, p. 27, p. 41, p. 42 | V | weak |
117	| RQ3 | Authors argue agentic solutions are architecturally more complex and "potentially more difficult to maintain"; maintainability not directly measured | p. 35 | A | weak |
118	| RQ4 | Evaluation used spec-derived category-partition oracle tests, MCC, coverage, LCS/LED similarity, iterations and time, with Kruskal-Wallis, one-tailed Mann-Whitney, Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni | p. 10, p. 11, p. 14 | V | moderate |
119	| RQ4 | Sample: 9 solo vs 7 collaborative professionals, 3 fully-automated and 12 agentic runs; 2 small Python tasks; time self-reported for humans but measured for automated runs | p. 12, p. 13, p. 16, p. 42 | V | moderate |
120	
121	## 14. Key quotes
122	> "The solutions produced by the agentic workflow show the highest functional correctness, although human developers can reach the same level of correctness in collaborative settings." (p. 26)
123	
124	> "autonomous agentic platforms can effectively solve development tasks while generating solutions that are architecturally more complex and potentially more difficult to maintain" (p. 35)
125	
126	> "Nonetheless, the limited number of professional participants reduces the statistical power of our analyses." (p. 36)
127	
128	## Analyst notes
129	- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1-43), including appendix Table 16 (pp. 41-42) and declarations (p. 43). Fig. 4 (task specification, p. 12) and Table 7 (prompts, p. 20) read from the PDF images because the text layer omits them. Figures 1-3, 5-11 (diagrams/boxplots) not inspected beyond captions and text. Reference list (pp. 43-48) only checked for the replication package. Replication package not opened.
130	- Uncertainties: whether "randomly assigned" (p. 15) applied to all 16 or only to the 11 new participants is not stated. Agentic TPR values in Table 16 (83.0, 92.0) do not exactly equal multiples of 1/12 (83.3, 91.7), suggesting rounding or a different baseline count for agentic runs; not explained. # Full text extracted from paper.pdf by pdftotext.
# [PDF page N] = Nth page of the PDF file, which may differ from the printed page number.


=== [PDF page 1] ===

Empirical Software Engineering      (2027) 32:40
https://doi.org/10.1007/s10664-026-10950-z




Vibe Coding: An experiment with test-driven development

Moritz Mock1        · Barbara Russo1

Received: 27 October 2025 / Accepted: 4 August 2026
© The Author(s) 2026


Abstract
Context Conversational Large Language Models (CLLMs) can automatically generate
code by collaborating with users through natural language. However, poor collaboration
can lead to poor quality output.
 Objective This exploratory study aims to investigate how humans and CLLMs can col-
laborate as peers through vibe coding, an approach that integrates principles from prompt
engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation to enhance collaboration.
 Method We designed four interaction models representing different collaboration patterns
in the software development process: the solo model (human-only development), the col-
laborative model (human–CLLM collaboration), the fully automated model (development
autonomously performed by a CLLM), and the agentic model (development autonomously
performed by the MetaGPT X platform). Based on these models, we implemented corre-
sponding Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflows using structured prompts and Python
scripts. We then conducted a controlled pre-experimental study with TDD professionals to
compare the solo and collaborative workflows. In addition, we performed repeated explor-
atory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on the same development tasks
to obtain complementary evidence.
 Results Our findings suggest that the choice of interaction model should depend on the
development objective. Agentic workflows are best suited for rapid development and func-
tionally correct production code but may introduce additional implementation complexity.

34	
35	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses

40	
41	## 3. Methodology

Prompts built from White et al.'s prompt-pattern catalogue (Game Play, Persona, Template, Context Manager, Question Refinement) (p. 8); prompts tell the CLLM "Built-in functions are not allowed" (Table 7, p. 20). 52	## 5. Experimental setup

97	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Simple tasks, single CLLM for human workflows (p. 37). [I] Python-only, function-level tasks, one agentic platform; results do not transfer to multi-file applications or UI work.
98	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] TPR against a 12-assertion spec-derived suite is a reasonable small-scale functional-correctness oracle; MCC alone is a thin proxy for maintainability; lower baseline coverage of agentic code partly reflects added validation/logging rather than lower quality.
99	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] Holm-Bonferroni correction and effect sizes reported (p. 10, p. 11). [A] Low power acknowledged (p. 36). [I] Non-independent repeated runs pooled as samples; no confidence intervals; one-tailed tests chosen for every direction.
100	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Prompts (Table 7, p. 20), metrics definitions (p. 14), per-participant data (p. 41, p. 42) and GitHub package (p. 43). [I] Agentic runs via a web interface of a commercial platform are hard to reproduce; model parameters not reported.
101	
102	## 11. Future research directions
103	- Stated by authors [A]: extend to other development practices, CLLMs and agentic platforms (p. 40); investigate whether phase-based and iterative process models remain appropriate when AI can generate complete solutions (p. 40); apply the fully-automated evaluation suite to MBPP and HumanEval (p. 40); study agentic performance under different prompting settings (p. 17); more integrated experimental platforms than Colab (p. 34).
104	- Suggested by us [I]: hold the model constant across workflows; use larger, application-level tasks; measure maintainability with more than MCC (e.g. static-analysis smells, change effort); for our project, reuse the idea of a specification-derived oracle test suite (category-partition) as a functional-fidelity measure for a reconstructed app.
105	
106	## 12. Relevance to our research
107	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (contrasts structured vibe coding with agentic generation), RQ2 (functional correctness measured by a spec-derived baseline test suite), RQ3 (complexity and coverage of AI-generated vs human code), RQ4 (design weaknesses: tiny N, model confound, mixed measurement), RQ5 (no application-level or maintainability-focused evaluation).
108	- How it informs our work [I]: one of the few peer-reviewed controlled experiments that labels its condition "vibe coding" and compares it with human-only and agentic generation. Its evaluation framework (oracle tests for correctness + complexity/coverage for internal quality + time/iterations for effort) is a template our study design could scale up. Its findings are function-level and confounded, so they should not be used as evidence about application reconstruction. Relevance medium for RQ4/RQ5 design lessons, low for direct outcome evidence.
109

114	| RQ2 | Agentic runs passed more spec-derived baseline tests (mean TPR 94.58%) than solo (62.0%), collaborative (60.8%) and fully-automated (83.3%) workflows; significant after Holm-Bonferroni, but agentic used newer models (GPT-5/Claude Sonnet 4 vs GPT-3.5 Turbo) | p. 25, p. 41, p. 42 | V | weak |
115	| RQ2 | Collaborative vibe coding did not differ significantly from solo human coding in functional correctness (TPR p = 0.314); human results varied from 8.3% to 100% | p. 25, p. 41 | V | weak |
116	| RQ3 | Agentic code had higher McCabe complexity (mean 11.67 vs about 6-6.6 for other workflows) and lower baseline branch coverage (65.3% vs 79-84% for human workflows), adding helpers, logging and validation | p. 24, p. 27, p. 41, p. 42 | V | weak |
117	| RQ3 | Authors argue agentic solutions are architecturally more complex and "potentially more difficult to maintain"; maintainability not directly measured | p. 35 | A | weak |
118	| RQ4 | Evaluation used spec-derived category-partition oracle tests, MCC, coverage, LCS/LED similarity, iterations and time, with Kruskal-Wallis, one-tailed Mann-Whitney, Cliff's delta and Holm-Bonferroni | p. 10, p. 11, p. 14 | V | moderate |

Vibe Coding: An experiment with test-driven development

Moritz Mock1        · Barbara Russo1

Received: 27 October 2025 / Accepted: 4 August 2026
© The Author(s) 2026


Abstract
Context Conversational Large Language Models (CLLMs) can automatically generate
code by collaborating with users through natural language. However, poor collaboration
can lead to poor quality output.
 Objective This exploratory study aims to investigate how humans and CLLMs can col-
laborate as peers through vibe coding, an approach that integrates principles from prompt
engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation to enhance collaboration.
 Method We designed four interaction models representing different collaboration patterns
in the software development process: the solo model (human-only development), the col-
laborative model (human–CLLM collaboration), the fully automated model (development
autonomously performed by a CLLM), and the agentic model (development autonomously
performed by the MetaGPT X platform). Based on these models, we implemented corre-
sponding Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflows using structured prompts and Python
scripts. We then conducted a controlled pre-experimental study with TDD professionals to
compare the solo and collaborative workflows. In addition, we performed repeated explor-
atory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on the same development tasks
to obtain complementary evidence.
 Results Our findings suggest that the choice of interaction model should depend on the
development objective. Agentic workflows are best suited for rapid development and func-
tionally correct production code but may introduce additional implementation complexity.

18	# Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable & Reliable Than Human-Written Code?
19	
20	- Authors: Molison, Alfred Santa; Moraes, Marcia; Melo, Glaucia; Santos, Fabio; Assunção, Wesley K. G.
21	- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The PDF is the arXiv version (arXiv:2508.00700v1); page numbers refer to our PDF, not the ESEM proceedings pagination.
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Compare internal quality attributes (maintainability and reliability) of LLM-generated and human-written Python code, including the SonarQube-estimated effort to fix issues, across three task difficulty levels and three LLM configurations (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuning) (p. 1).
30	- [A] Secondary aim: provide a reusable experimentation infrastructure (LLM + PostgreSQL + SonarQube) for replications and automated quality analysis (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [V] Single RQ: "Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable and Reliable than Human-Written Code?" (p. 1).
34	- [V] The only explicit null hypothesis is H0 of equal effort-in-minutes distributions between groups (p. 7, p. 9). No hypotheses are stated for bugs or code smells; these are compared with odds ratios (p. 6).
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Quantitative comparative study (static analysis of four solution sets) plus a small manual functional-correctness check (Pass@1) and qualitative inspection of failures (p. 3, p. 5, p. 8).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] GPT-4o-2024-08-06 via the OpenAI API, used in three configurations: zero-shot prompt, few-shot prompt, and a fine-tuned GPT-4o (p. 4). The authors call all three "prompt engineering techniques" (p. 4).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Human solutions from the APPS dataset serve as the baseline ("the human dataset") (p. 4). Pairwise comparisons: each LLM configuration vs human, few-shot vs zero-shot, fine-tuned vs zero-shot (p. 6, p. 8). Few-shot vs fine-tuned is not reported.
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] APPS dataset (Hendrycks et al., NeurIPS 2021): 10,000 Python coding questions with multiple human solutions per question, labelled introductory, interview or competition (p. 3, p. 11). Human solutions were collected from Codeforces, AtCoder, Kattis and Codewars and curated by students over six months (p. 3–4).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit:
44	  - [V] Fine-tuning: 80 random questions per level for training (240 total); 160 questions per level for testing (480 total) (p. 4).
45	  - Number of questions submitted for zero-shot and few-shot generation: not reported (the text says "each coding question" was submitted, p. 4, but does not say whether this means all 10,000 or the 480 test questions).
46	  - Number of human solutions analysed by SonarQube: not reported. APPS has several human solutions per question (p. 3); whether all, one, or a sample were used is not stated.
47	  - [V] Twelve SonarQube result files (4 datasets × 3 difficulty levels) (p. 5).
48	  - [V] Pass@1 evaluated on 15 solutions per approach, 5 per difficulty level (p. 7–8).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Fine-tuning training questions were drawn at random (p. 4). [A] The performance sample was "randomized" and "representative" (p. 10). Whether the 480 test questions were disjoint from the 240 training questions: not reported.
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] APPS is public; replication package on Zenodo (record 15283737) (p. 1, p. 11).
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
54	  - [V] Model GPT-4o-2024-08-06, chosen as the latest model that allowed fine-tuning; temperature 1.00, max tokens 2048, top-p 1.00, frequency and presence penalties 0.00 (p. 4).
55	  - [V] Zero-shot prompt: "Generate a Python code (only one solution) to solve this question:" plus the problem text (p. 4).
56	  - [V] Few-shot prompt: the question followed by all human solutions for that same question from APPS ("Sample Solution {index}" entries) (p. 4).
57	  - [V] Fine-tuning: GPT base model trained on 240 question–answer pairs; training loss 0.21; 496,176 tokens (p. 4). Epochs and other fine-tuning hyper-parameters not reported.
58	  - Number of generations per question: not reported (one solution per prompt is implied by the zero-shot prompt wording, p. 4). Repeated runs or seeds: not reported.
59	  - [V] SonarQube Free Server edition, default Python quality profile and quality gate; a new SonarQube project is created before each scan so that all files count as new code; scans driven by Python scripts via SonarScanner CLI; results stored in PostgreSQL (p. 4–5).
60	  - SonarQube version: the docs link points to SonarQube Server 10.8 (p. 4); exact installed version not otherwise reported.
61	  - [V] Infrastructure: Ubuntu Linux VM in a VPC with SonarQube, Grafana, PostgreSQL and Python (p. 3).
62	  - [V] Pass@1: three authors ran sampled solutions with `python3 file.py`, fed inputs from the test cases in the problem description, and checked outputs (p. 5, p. 8).
63	- Code availability: [V] Scripts and replication package available on Zenodo (p. 3, p. 11).
64	
65	## 6. Evaluation metrics
66	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
67	  - [V] SonarQube Bugs (reliability: coding errors causing runtime failures or unexpected behaviour), Vulnerabilities (security), Code Smells (maintainability) (p. 5).
68	  - [V] Severity levels Blocker, Critical, Major, Minor (p. 5).
69	  - [V] Effort-in-minutes: SonarQube's estimated time to fix issues (p. 5).
70	  - [V] Normalised issue percentage per dataset ("proportion of rows") (p. 5–6).
71	  - [V] Pass@1 (Chen et al. formula), k = 1 (p. 5).
72	  - [A] Metrics were chosen because prior studies used reliability, maintainability and security, and SonarQube is a standard static-analysis tool (p. 2–3).
73	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
74	  - [V] Effort: Mann-Whitney U test with Cliff's delta, Romano et al. thresholds (negligible < 0.147, small < 0.33, medium < 0.474, else large) (p. 5).
75	  - [V] Bugs and code smells: odds ratios from 2×2 contingency tables per comparison, with significance stars (p. 5–6, p. 8). The test that produced the p-values for the odds ratios is not named.
76	  - Confidence intervals: not reported. Correction for multiple comparisons: not reported (15 comparisons per table across Tables II–IV, p. 8). Power analysis: not reported.
77	
78	## 7. Key findings
79	1. [V] SonarQube found no security vulnerabilities in any dataset (p. 5).
80	2. [V] Odds of a SonarQube bug in LLM solutions vs human solutions were very low in every configuration and level: zero-shot 0.008 / 0.006 / 0.0005, few-shot 0.003 / 0.006 / 0.001, fine-tuned 0.00 / 0.019 / 0.0005 (introductory / interview / competition), all p < 0.001 (Table II, p. 8).
81	3. [V] Code smells were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human for introductory problems (p < 0.001); few-shot vs human was 0.52 for competition (p < 0.05); fine-tuned vs human was 0.00 for introductory and competition (p < 0.001); several other comparisons were not significant (Table III, p. 8).
82	4. [V] In the human dataset, bug-type issues were dominated by Blocker severity (87.50% introductory, 71.27% interview, 86.30% competition, Table I) (p. 8). [A] The authors interpret these as "bug rates" (p. 6).
83	5. [V] Average SonarQube effort to fix (min): introductory human 7.20, zero-shot 3.75, few-shot 4.72, fine-tuned 5.00; interview human 7.06, zero-shot 5.48, few-shot 6.13, fine-tuned 4.67; competition human 6.95, zero-shot 6.14, few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60 (Fig. 6, p. 7). [A] "LLMs reduced effort in simpler tasks, but this advantage diminished as the tasks became more complex" (p. 7).
84	6. [V] Cliff's delta for effort, zero-shot vs human: 0.54 large (introductory), 0.21 small (interview), 0.1 negligible (competition), all significant; fine-tuned vs human introductory 0.24 small and fine-tuned vs zero-shot introductory −0.50 large are not marked significant (Table IV, p. 8).
85	7. [V] Severity shift: for interview problems fine-tuning had 94.1% minor, 2.1% major, 1.2% critical, 2.6% blocker issues, vs human 10.7% blocker (p. 6). For competition problems the human dataset had the fewest critical issues relative to LLM outputs (p. 6). [A] LLMs "may introduce more critical issues compared to human-generated code" on competition tasks (Finding 3, p. 6).
86	8. [V] Pass@1 on 15 sampled solutions per approach: human 1.0, zero-shot 0.53, few-shot 0.87, fine-tuned 0.47 (Table V, p. 8). Partial (some test cases passed) solutions: 47% of zero-shot, 13% of few-shot and fine-tuned (p. 8). Failures included runtime errors, wrong outputs, hard-coded inputs, waiting for input indefinitely and syntax errors (p. 8).
87	9. [A] The fine-tuned model has "the best quality metrics" yet "struggled to generate code for complex solutions" (p. 8); the authors attribute its low performance to too few fine-tuning samples (p. 9).
88	10. [A] AI models "may better avoid functional bugs than address structural code quality concerns" (p. 9).
89	
90	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
91	- [A] Possible cross-contamination of coding patterns or prompts between instances, affecting comparisons across zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuned conditions (p. 10).
92	- [A] Prompt sensitivity: different wording could give significantly different results (p. 10).
93	- [A] Python only and competitive-programming style problems; limited generalisability to other languages and real-world software development (p. 10).
94	- [A] Only GPT-4 (GPT-4o) and a fine-tuned version; may not represent other LLMs (p. 10).
95	- [A] APPS lacks contextual information about the human-written code (p. 10).
96	- [A] Performance sample may not represent the population (p. 10).
97	- [A] LLM parameter and token-limit variations were not tested (p. 10).
98	- [A] SonarQube metrics may not capture all aspects of quality; its effort estimates may not reflect real developer effort (p. 10).
99	- [A] Fine-tuning used a limited number of rows due to resource constraints (p. 10).
100	
101	## 9. Limitations we identified
102	- [I] Few-shot leakage: the few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions to the same question (p. 4). Few-shot outputs can therefore copy or adapt the baseline itself, so few-shot vs human is not an independent comparison and the high few-shot Pass@1 (0.87, p. 8) may partly reflect this. Based on the prompt description, p. 4.
103	- [I] Quality and correctness are not linked: static-quality comparisons include LLM solutions that fail the tests (fine-tuned Pass@1 0.47, p. 8). "Fewer bugs" in SonarQube terms is not "more correct" code. The headline "LLM-generated code has fewer bugs" (p. 1) uses SonarQube's rule-based "bug" category, not functional failures. Based on p. 5 and p. 8.
104	- [I] Unit of analysis and denominators unclear: the number of human solutions and of zero-/few-shot solutions analysed is not reported (p. 3–4), and normalised percentages are described as "proportion of rows" (p. 5) without defining a row. Odds ratios therefore cannot be reconstructed from the paper.
105	- [I] Baseline quality: APPS human solutions are competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability, as the authors themselves note (p. 9). They are a weak and possibly unfair baseline for maintainability claims.
106	- [I] Data contamination: APPS has been public since 2021 (p. 11), so GPT-4o may have seen its problems and solutions in training. The paper does not discuss this; its "cross-contamination" limitation (p. 10) concerns prompts, not training data.
107	- [I] Single sample per question at temperature 1.0 (p. 4), with no repeated runs, so run-to-run variance is unknown.
108	- [I] Pass@1 on 15 solutions per approach (p. 7–8) is too small to support the performance ranking (e.g. 0.87 vs 0.53).
109	- [I] Internal inconsistencies:
110	  - Few-shot Pass@1 is 0.86 in the introduction (p. 1) and 0.87 in Table V (p. 8).
111	  - Finding 7 says odds of bugs are "≤ 0.19%" (p. 9), but Table II includes 0.019, i.e. 1.9% (p. 8).
112	  - Several severity percentages in the text do not match Fig. 5. Examples: zero-shot introductory critical is 5.0% in the text (p. 5) but 6.6 in Fig. 5 (p. 7); few-shot introductory values (critical 9.8%, major 40.2%, p. 5) do not appear in Fig. 5, where that bar is empty (p. 7); fine-tuned competition minor is 30% in the text (p. 6) but Fig. 5 shows 40.0 (p. 7).
113	  - The code-smell paragraph says "a bug in a few-shot approach is half as likely as a bug in a human solution" (p. 7), mixing bugs with smells.
114	  - The limitations say "GPT-4" (p. 10) while the model is GPT-4o (p. 4).
115	- [I] Top-p = 1.0 is described as "ensuring the most probable token distributions were used" (p. 4); top-p = 1.0 in fact applies no nucleus truncation. Minor, but it shows imprecise reporting of the generation setup.
116	
117	## 10. Threats to validity
118	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Few-shot prompts contain baseline solutions (p. 4). Possible training-data contamination with APPS (not discussed). Train/test disjointness for fine-tuning not reported (p. 4). The human baseline includes many solutions per question, while LLMs produce one, so issue counts per question are not comparable unless normalised. The normalisation is not fully specified (p. 5).
119	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Python, algorithmic problems, one model family (p. 10). [I] Single-function stdin/stdout programs say little about multi-file applications, UIs or vibe-coded apps.
120	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [A] SonarQube rules and effort estimates are proxies (p. 10). [I] Static "bugs" and "code smells" from the default profile are only a partial measure of maintainability. Effort-to-fix is SonarQube's rule-based remediation estimate, not a measured effort.
121	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] No CIs and no multiple-comparison correction (p. 8). [I] Odds ratios of 0.00 imply zero cells, where ORs are undefined without correction. A large Cliff's delta (−0.50) that is not significant suggests small or tied samples for the fine-tuned introductory set (p. 8).
122	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Replication package with scripts on Zenodo, public dataset, model version and decoding parameters reported (p. 4, p. 11). [I] Sample sizes per condition, fine-tuning hyper-parameters, the exact SonarQube version and the OR test are missing. Fine-tuned GPT-4o weights are proprietary, so exact regeneration may be impossible.
123	
124	## 11. Future research directions
125	- Stated by authors [A]:
126	  - Explore parameter tuning (p. 10).
127	  - Use PEFT and data pruning instead of costly full fine-tuning (p. 9).
128	  - Study quality–performance–cost trade-offs in different domains (p. 10).
129	  - Try RAG and other LLMs; add more languages and quality metrics (p. 10).
130	  - Add a component that checks solution performance (p. 10).
131	  - Study links to educational outcomes (p. 10).
132	- Suggested by us [I]:
133	  - Report static quality only for solutions that pass the tests, so quality and correctness are evaluated jointly.
134	  - Use several samples per task with variance reporting.
135	  - Use a baseline of maintained, production-style human code.
136	  - Apply the same SonarQube pipeline to multi-file, application-level outputs (e.g. vibe-coded web apps) instead of single-function programs.
137	
138	## 12. Relevance to our research
139	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (primary), RQ4, RQ2 (minor), RQ5.
140	- How it informs our work [I]:
141	  - It is a peer-reviewed (ESEM) direct comparison of LLM vs human code quality using SonarQube. It is a candidate template for the code-quality arm of a reconstruction study: default quality profile, bugs, smells, severity and remediation effort.
142	  - It shows that static quality and functional correctness can diverge sharply: the fine-tuned model has the best quality metrics but the lowest Pass@1. Any evaluation of reconstructed applications must therefore measure fidelity and quality jointly.
143	  - Its weaknesses are useful design lessons for RQ4/RQ5: baseline leakage, unreported N, tiny correctness sample, and no CIs or multiple-comparison correction.
144	  - Relevance is medium rather than high because the tasks are algorithmic snippets, not applications reconstructed from observable behaviour.
145	
146	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
147	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
148	|---|---|---|---|---|
149	| RQ3 | GPT-4o solutions (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuned) had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged bugs than APPS human solutions at all difficulty levels (OR 0.0005–0.019, p<0.001) | 8 | V | weak (single model and study; N per group not reported; few-shot prompt contains baseline solutions) |
150	| RQ3 | Code-smell (maintainability) differences were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human on introductory tasks, while fine-tuned had fewer smells; several comparisons were not significant | 8 | V | weak |
151	| RQ3 | SonarQube-estimated fix effort was lower for LLM code on introductory/interview tasks but not on competition tasks (human 6.95 min vs few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60) | 7 | V | weak |
152	| RQ3 | On competition-level problems LLM outputs carried more critical-severity issues than human code | 6 | A | weak |
153	| RQ2 | Functional correctness diverged from static quality: Pass@1 human 1.0, few-shot 0.87, zero-shot 0.53, fine-tuned 0.47 (fine-tuned had the best quality metrics) | 8 | V | weak (15 solutions per approach) |

14	     status: draft (in progress) -> ready (analyst self-check passed) -> complete (critical review passed).
15	     evidence_basis: full-text | abstract-only. abstract-only analyses must not fill methodology detail.

17	
18	# Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable & Reliable Than Human-Written Code?
19	
20	- Authors: Molison, Alfred Santa; Moraes, Marcia; Melo, Glaucia; Santos, Fabio; Assunção, Wesley K. G.
21	- Year / venue: 2025, 2025 ACM/IEEE International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM) (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1109/esem64174.2025.00036
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The PDF is the arXiv version (arXiv:2508.00700v1); page numbers refer to our PDF, not the ESEM proceedings pagination.
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Compare internal quality attributes (maintainability and reliability) of LLM-generated and human-written Python code, including the SonarQube-estimated effort to fix issues, across three task difficulty levels and three LLM configurations (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuning) (p. 1).
30	- [A] Secondary aim: provide a reusable experimentation infrastructure (LLM + PostgreSQL + SonarQube) for replications and automated quality analysis (p. 1).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [V] Single RQ: "Is LLM-Generated Code More Maintainable and Reliable than Human-Written Code?" (p. 1).
34	- [V] The only explicit null hypothesis is H0 of equal effort-in-minutes distributions between groups (p. 7, p. 9). No hypotheses are stated for bugs or code smells; these are compared with odds ratios (p. 6).
35	
36	## 3. Methodology
37	- Research design: [V] Quantitative comparative study (static analysis of four solution sets) plus a small manual functional-correctness check (Pass@1) and qualitative inspection of failures (p. 3, p. 5, p. 8).
38	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] GPT-4o-2024-08-06 via the OpenAI API, used in three configurations: zero-shot prompt, few-shot prompt, and a fine-tuned GPT-4o (p. 4). The authors call all three "prompt engineering techniques" (p. 4).
39	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] Human solutions from the APPS dataset serve as the baseline ("the human dataset") (p. 4). Pairwise comparisons: each LLM configuration vs human, few-shot vs zero-shot, fine-tuned vs zero-shot (p. 6, p. 8). Few-shot vs fine-tuned is not reported.
40	
41	## 4. Dataset and sample
42	- Data source(s): [V] APPS dataset (Hendrycks et al., NeurIPS 2021): 10,000 Python coding questions with multiple human solutions per question, labelled introductory, interview or competition (p. 3, p. 11). Human solutions were collected from Codeforces, AtCoder, Kattis and Codewars and curated by students over six months (p. 3–4).
43	- Sample size (N) and unit:
44	  - [V] Fine-tuning: 80 random questions per level for training (240 total); 160 questions per level for testing (480 total) (p. 4).
45	  - Number of questions submitted for zero-shot and few-shot generation: not reported (the text says "each coding question" was submitted, p. 4, but does not say whether this means all 10,000 or the 480 test questions).
46	  - Number of human solutions analysed by SonarQube: not reported. APPS has several human solutions per question (p. 3); whether all, one, or a sample were used is not stated.
47	  - [V] Twelve SonarQube result files (4 datasets × 3 difficulty levels) (p. 5).
48	  - [V] Pass@1 evaluated on 15 solutions per approach, 5 per difficulty level (p. 7–8).
49	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Fine-tuning training questions were drawn at random (p. 4). [A] The performance sample was "randomized" and "representative" (p. 10). Whether the 480 test questions were disjoint from the 240 training questions: not reported.
50	- Data availability (public? link?): [V] APPS is public; replication package on Zenodo (record 15283737) (p. 1, p. 11).
51	
52	## 5. Experimental setup
53	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
54	  - [V] Model GPT-4o-2024-08-06, chosen as the latest model that allowed fine-tuning; temperature 1.00, max tokens 2048, top-p 1.00, frequency and presence penalties 0.00 (p. 4).
55	  - [V] Zero-shot prompt: "Generate a Python code (only one solution) to solve this question:" plus the problem text (p. 4).
56	  - [V] Few-shot prompt: the question followed by all human solutions for that same question from APPS ("Sample Solution {index}" entries) (p. 4).
57	  - [V] Fine-tuning: GPT base model trained on 240 question–answer pairs; training loss 0.21; 496,176 tokens (p. 4). Epochs and other fine-tuning hyper-parameters not reported.
58	  - Number of generations per question: not reported (one solution per prompt is implied by the zero-shot prompt wording, p. 4). Repeated runs or seeds: not reported.
59	  - [V] SonarQube Free Server edition, default Python quality profile and quality gate; a new SonarQube project is created before each scan so that all files count as new code; scans driven by Python scripts via SonarScanner CLI; results stored in PostgreSQL (p. 4–5).
60	  - SonarQube version: the docs link points to SonarQube Server 10.8 (p. 4); exact installed version not otherwise reported.
61	  - [V] Infrastructure: Ubuntu Linux VM in a VPC with SonarQube, Grafana, PostgreSQL and Python (p. 3).
62	  - [V] Pass@1: three authors ran sampled solutions with `python3 file.py`, fed inputs from the test cases in the problem description, and checked outputs (p. 5, p. 8).
63	- Code availability: [V] Scripts and replication package available on Zenodo (p. 3, p. 11).
64	
65	## 6. Evaluation metrics
66	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
67	  - [V] SonarQube Bugs (reliability: coding errors causing runtime failures or unexpected behaviour), Vulnerabilities (security), Code Smells (maintainability) (p. 5).
68	  - [V] Severity levels Blocker, Critical, Major, Minor (p. 5).
69	  - [V] Effort-in-minutes: SonarQube's estimated time to fix issues (p. 5).
70	  - [V] Normalised issue percentage per dataset ("proportion of rows") (p. 5–6).
71	  - [V] Pass@1 (Chen et al. formula), k = 1 (p. 5).
72	  - [A] Metrics were chosen because prior studies used reliability, maintainability and security, and SonarQube is a standard static-analysis tool (p. 2–3).
73	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals):
74	  - [V] Effort: Mann-Whitney U test with Cliff's delta, Romano et al. thresholds (negligible < 0.147, small < 0.33, medium < 0.474, else large) (p. 5).
75	  - [V] Bugs and code smells: odds ratios from 2×2 contingency tables per comparison, with significance stars (p. 5–6, p. 8). The test that produced the p-values for the odds ratios is not named.
76	  - Confidence intervals: not reported. Correction for multiple comparisons: not reported (15 comparisons per table across Tables II–IV, p. 8). Power analysis: not reported.
77	
78	## 7. Key findings
79	1. [V] SonarQube found no security vulnerabilities in any dataset (p. 5).
80	2. [V] Odds of a SonarQube bug in LLM solutions vs human solutions were very low in every configuration and level: zero-shot 0.008 / 0.006 / 0.0005, few-shot 0.003 / 0.006 / 0.001, fine-tuned 0.00 / 0.019 / 0.0005 (introductory / interview / competition), all p < 0.001 (Table II, p. 8).
81	3. [V] Code smells were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human for introductory problems (p < 0.001); few-shot vs human was 0.52 for competition (p < 0.05); fine-tuned vs human was 0.00 for introductory and competition (p < 0.001); several other comparisons were not significant (Table III, p. 8).
82	4. [V] In the human dataset, bug-type issues were dominated by Blocker severity (87.50% introductory, 71.27% interview, 86.30% competition, Table I) (p. 8). [A] The authors interpret these as "bug rates" (p. 6).
83	5. [V] Average SonarQube effort to fix (min): introductory human 7.20, zero-shot 3.75, few-shot 4.72, fine-tuned 5.00; interview human 7.06, zero-shot 5.48, few-shot 6.13, fine-tuned 4.67; competition human 6.95, zero-shot 6.14, few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60 (Fig. 6, p. 7). [A] "LLMs reduced effort in simpler tasks, but this advantage diminished as the tasks became more complex" (p. 7).
84	6. [V] Cliff's delta for effort, zero-shot vs human: 0.54 large (introductory), 0.21 small (interview), 0.1 negligible (competition), all significant; fine-tuned vs human introductory 0.24 small and fine-tuned vs zero-shot introductory −0.50 large are not marked significant (Table IV, p. 8).
85	7. [V] Severity shift: for interview problems fine-tuning had 94.1% minor, 2.1% major, 1.2% critical, 2.6% blocker issues, vs human 10.7% blocker (p. 6). For competition problems the human dataset had the fewest critical issues relative to LLM outputs (p. 6). [A] LLMs "may introduce more critical issues compared to human-generated code" on competition tasks (Finding 3, p. 6).
86	8. [V] Pass@1 on 15 sampled solutions per approach: human 1.0, zero-shot 0.53, few-shot 0.87, fine-tuned 0.47 (Table V, p. 8). Partial (some test cases passed) solutions: 47% of zero-shot, 13% of few-shot and fine-tuned (p. 8). Failures included runtime errors, wrong outputs, hard-coded inputs, waiting for input indefinitely and syntax errors (p. 8).
87	9. [A] The fine-tuned model has "the best quality metrics" yet "struggled to generate code for complex solutions" (p. 8); the authors attribute its low performance to too few fine-tuning samples (p. 9).
88	10. [A] AI models "may better avoid functional bugs than address structural code quality concerns" (p. 9).
89	
90	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
91	- [A] Possible cross-contamination of coding patterns or prompts between instances, affecting comparisons across zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuned conditions (p. 10).
92	- [A] Prompt sensitivity: different wording could give significantly different results (p. 10).
93	- [A] Python only and competitive-programming style problems; limited generalisability to other languages and real-world software development (p. 10).
94	- [A] Only GPT-4 (GPT-4o) and a fine-tuned version; may not represent other LLMs (p. 10).
95	- [A] APPS lacks contextual information about the human-written code (p. 10).
96	- [A] Performance sample may not represent the population (p. 10).
97	- [A] LLM parameter and token-limit variations were not tested (p. 10).
98	- [A] SonarQube metrics may not capture all aspects of quality; its effort estimates may not reflect real developer effort (p. 10).
99	- [A] Fine-tuning used a limited number of rows due to resource constraints (p. 10).
100	
101	## 9. Limitations we identified
102	- [I] Few-shot leakage: the few-shot prompt contains the human reference solutions to the same question (p. 4). Few-shot outputs can therefore copy or adapt the baseline itself, so few-shot vs human is not an independent comparison and the high few-shot Pass@1 (0.87, p. 8) may partly reflect this. Based on the prompt description, p. 4.
103	- [I] Quality and correctness are not linked: static-quality comparisons include LLM solutions that fail the tests (fine-tuned Pass@1 0.47, p. 8). "Fewer bugs" in SonarQube terms is not "more correct" code. The headline "LLM-generated code has fewer bugs" (p. 1) uses SonarQube's rule-based "bug" category, not functional failures. Based on p. 5 and p. 8.
104	- [I] Unit of analysis and denominators unclear: the number of human solutions and of zero-/few-shot solutions analysed is not reported (p. 3–4), and normalised percentages are described as "proportion of rows" (p. 5) without defining a row. Odds ratios therefore cannot be reconstructed from the paper.
105	- [I] Baseline quality: APPS human solutions are competitive-programming submissions written for correctness, not maintainability, as the authors themselves note (p. 9). They are a weak and possibly unfair baseline for maintainability claims.
106	- [I] Data contamination: APPS has been public since 2021 (p. 11), so GPT-4o may have seen its problems and solutions in training. The paper does not discuss this; its "cross-contamination" limitation (p. 10) concerns prompts, not training data.
107	- [I] Single sample per question at temperature 1.0 (p. 4), with no repeated runs, so run-to-run variance is unknown.
108	- [I] Pass@1 on 15 solutions per approach (p. 7–8) is too small to support the performance ranking (e.g. 0.87 vs 0.53).
109	- [I] Internal inconsistencies:
110	  - Few-shot Pass@1 is 0.86 in the introduction (p. 1) and 0.87 in Table V (p. 8).
111	  - Finding 7 says odds of bugs are "≤ 0.19%" (p. 9), but Table II includes 0.019, i.e. 1.9% (p. 8).
112	  - Several severity percentages in the text do not match Fig. 5. Examples: zero-shot introductory critical is 5.0% in the text (p. 5) but 6.6 in Fig. 5 (p. 7); few-shot introductory values (critical 9.8%, major 40.2%, p. 5) do not appear in Fig. 5, where that bar is empty (p. 7); fine-tuned competition minor is 30% in the text (p. 6) but Fig. 5 shows 40.0 (p. 7).
113	  - The code-smell paragraph says "a bug in a few-shot approach is half as likely as a bug in a human solution" (p. 7), mixing bugs with smells.
114	  - The limitations say "GPT-4" (p. 10) while the model is GPT-4o (p. 4).
115	- [I] Top-p = 1.0 is described as "ensuring the most probable token distributions were used" (p. 4); top-p = 1.0 in fact applies no nucleus truncation. Minor, but it shows imprecise reporting of the generation setup.
116	
117	## 10. Threats to validity
118	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Few-shot prompts contain baseline solutions (p. 4). Possible training-data contamination with APPS (not discussed). Train/test disjointness for fine-tuning not reported (p. 4). The human baseline includes many solutions per question, while LLMs produce one, so issue counts per question are not comparable unless normalised. The normalisation is not fully specified (p. 5).
119	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [A] Python, algorithmic problems, one model family (p. 10). [I] Single-function stdin/stdout programs say little about multi-file applications, UIs or vibe-coded apps.
120	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [A] SonarQube rules and effort estimates are proxies (p. 10). [I] Static "bugs" and "code smells" from the default profile are only a partial measure of maintainability. Effort-to-fix is SonarQube's rule-based remediation estimate, not a measured effort.
121	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [V] No CIs and no multiple-comparison correction (p. 8). [I] Odds ratios of 0.00 imply zero cells, where ORs are undefined without correction. A large Cliff's delta (−0.50) that is not significant suggests small or tied samples for the fine-tuned introductory set (p. 8).
122	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [V] Replication package with scripts on Zenodo, public dataset, model version and decoding parameters reported (p. 4, p. 11). [I] Sample sizes per condition, fine-tuning hyper-parameters, the exact SonarQube version and the OR test are missing. Fine-tuned GPT-4o weights are proprietary, so exact regeneration may be impossible.
123	
124	## 11. Future research directions
125	- Stated by authors [A]:
126	  - Explore parameter tuning (p. 10).
127	  - Use PEFT and data pruning instead of costly full fine-tuning (p. 9).
128	  - Study quality–performance–cost trade-offs in different domains (p. 10).
129	  - Try RAG and other LLMs; add more languages and quality metrics (p. 10).
130	  - Add a component that checks solution performance (p. 10).
131	  - Study links to educational outcomes (p. 10).
132	- Suggested by us [I]:
133	  - Report static quality only for solutions that pass the tests, so quality and correctness are evaluated jointly.
134	  - Use several samples per task with variance reporting.
135	  - Use a baseline of maintained, production-style human code.
136	  - Apply the same SonarQube pipeline to multi-file, application-level outputs (e.g. vibe-coded web apps) instead of single-function programs.
137	
138	## 12. Relevance to our research
139	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ3 (primary), RQ4, RQ2 (minor), RQ5.
140	- How it informs our work [I]:
141	  - It is a peer-reviewed (ESEM) direct comparison of LLM vs human code quality using SonarQube. It is a candidate template for the code-quality arm of a reconstruction study: default quality profile, bugs, smells, severity and remediation effort.
142	  - It shows that static quality and functional correctness can diverge sharply: the fine-tuned model has the best quality metrics but the lowest Pass@1. Any evaluation of reconstructed applications must therefore measure fidelity and quality jointly.
143	  - Its weaknesses are useful design lessons for RQ4/RQ5: baseline leakage, unreported N, tiny correctness sample, and no CIs or multiple-comparison correction.
144	  - Relevance is medium rather than high because the tasks are algorithmic snippets, not applications reconstructed from observable behaviour.
145	
146	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
147	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
148	|---|---|---|---|---|
149	| RQ3 | GPT-4o solutions (zero-shot, few-shot, fine-tuned) had far lower odds of SonarQube-flagged bugs than APPS human solutions at all difficulty levels (OR 0.0005–0.019, p<0.001) | 8 | V | weak (single model and study; N per group not reported; few-shot prompt contains baseline solutions) |
150	| RQ3 | Code-smell (maintainability) differences were mixed: zero-shot had 3.57× the odds of a smell vs human on introductory tasks, while fine-tuned had fewer smells; several comparisons were not significant | 8 | V | weak |
151	| RQ3 | SonarQube-estimated fix effort was lower for LLM code on introductory/interview tasks but not on competition tasks (human 6.95 min vs few-shot 7.33, fine-tuned 7.60) | 7 | V | weak |
152	| RQ3 | On competition-level problems LLM outputs carried more critical-severity issues than human code | 6 | A | weak |
153	| RQ2 | Functional correctness diverged from static quality: Pass@1 human 1.0, few-shot 0.87, zero-shot 0.53, fine-tuned 0.47 (fine-tuned had the best quality metrics) | 8 | V | weak (15 solutions per approach) |
154	| RQ4 | Comparison used SonarQube default profile, odds ratios, and Mann-Whitney U with Cliff's delta, without CIs or multiple-comparison correction | 5, 8 | V | moderate |
155	| RQ4 | The few-shot prompt included the human reference solutions of the same question, so few-shot vs human is not an independent comparison | 4 | I | moderate (directly from method description) |
156	| RQ5 | Authors call for other LLMs, more languages and metrics, RAG and cost–quality trade-off studies | 10 | A | weak |
157	
158	## 14. Key quotes
159	> "LLM-generated code has fewer bugs and requires less effort to fix them overall." (p. 1)
160	
161	> "the fine-tuned model solutions lost performance (0.47) compared to the few-shot model (0.86) in Pass@1" (p. 1)
162	
163	> "current AI models may better avoid functional bugs than address structural code quality concerns." (p. 9)
164	
165	> "Since the questions are not intended for use in a professional environment, the solutions may be prepared to be correct in the first place, leaving quality metrics as a low priority or even unobserved." (p. 9)
166	
167	## Analyst notes
168	- Reading coverage: all 12 PDF pages read, including references. Figures 4–6 and Tables I–V were checked on the PDF images (pp. 6–8) because text extraction scrambled them. Figure 1 (architecture) was not inspected in detail; it is descriptive only.
169	- Uncertainties:
170	  - The exact number of solutions per dataset is not reported. This is the main obstacle to judging statistical strength.
171	  - Fig. 5 seems misaligned with its column labels, or the text reports different numbers; we report the text and table values and flag the mismatch.
172	  - We cite our arXiv PDF; the ESEM version may differ slightly.
